blocks.body:
\makecoverpage
\tableofcontents
\addtocontents{toc}{\setcounter{tocdepth}{1}}
\cleardoublepage
\resetacronyms

Museum visits are most meaningful when visitors connect emotionally with the art, and it is that emotional response which turns viewing into deeper engagement. Such responses leave measurable traces in the body, and gallery studies have used those traces to track how visitors responded to the art \citep{Trondle2012}. \ac{VR} makes those traces unusually easy to collect. The experience is already delivered through a head-mounted display, and a study visit adds wrist-worn sensors, so physiological signals arrive as a by-product of the visit. A guide with access to them could dwell on works that captivate the visitor, skip those that do not, and personalise the narrative in real time. This thesis investigates whether worn sensors alone can estimate the affective states of unseen visitors accurately enough to drive such adaptive behaviour.

The setting is a museum reconstructed in virtual reality: a reduced form of the ``HERE: Black in Rembrandt's Time'' exhibition, developed with the Rembrandthuis Museum, in which five paintings hang in a single room \citep{vanderKaaden2026}. Visitors explore it on foot at their own pace, and a conversational agent talks with them as they look, prompted by whichever painting their gaze settles on. It explains an artwork when they fixate on it, falls silent when interest wanes, and acts on the specific painting and \ac{AOI} attended at that moment, read directly from the gaze stream. Van der Kaaden collected the data analysed here in this environment, recording eye tracking, \ac{EDA}, \ac{HRV}, and speech alongside each visitor's own affect annotations. These conditions also constrain what is measurable. Unlike a laboratory study, a virtual museum cannot require visitors to remain seated, maintain continuous sensor contact, or complete a lengthy setup. Nor can it guarantee that every sensor functions throughout the visit.

Physiological emotion recognition has typically been studied in laboratory settings, with the field only recently shifting toward real-world, continuous monitoring \citep{Kumar2025}. Standard datasets such as DEAP \citep{Koelstra2012} and MAHNOB-HCI \citep{Soleymani2012} rely on clean, synchronised data that does not reflect the conditions of a real visit, in which sampling rates differ and walking introduces noise. Affective computing has been taken into \ac{VR} before, recognising emotion from wearable brain and cardiac signals \citep{MarinMoreales2018} and linking affect to the sense of presence \citep{Riva2007}. Those studies were typically run in controlled, seated setups rather than the free-roaming visit studied here. The nearest published comparison to this thesis is a free exploration of a real art exhibition and of a virtual replica of it, in which 15 of 60 participants were rejected for poor signal quality, and arousal and valence were classified under leave-one-subject-out validation at 71.52 and 77.08 per cent in the physical museum and at 75.00 and 71.08 per cent in the virtual one \citep{MarinMorales2019}. Their sensors are electroencephalography and chest electrocardiography only, with no electrodermal, eye-tracking or speech channel. Their target is a different object as well: a retrospective Self-Assessment Manikin rating given once per room and once per artwork, split into two classes, rather than a continuous per-second trace. Those accuracies are therefore two-class figures and are not comparable to a \ac{CCC}, and a museum study reaching 77 per cent is answering an easier question than the one asked here: which half of a scale a visitor endorsed after the visit, rather than where that visitor's rating stood at each second of it. This thesis shifts the focus from peak laboratory accuracy to what is recoverable in a moving, free-roaming setting.
Three technical challenges precede the analysis:
\noindent Each is addressed directly in the pipeline set out in Chapter~\ref{sec:methodology}.

A museum guide meets every visitor for the first time. Every question below is therefore posed under one constraint: each visitor is held out in turn, so no result rests on a person the model has already seen.

\medskip
\noindent\textbf{Primary Question:} How accurately can moment-to-moment valence and arousal be recovered for an unseen visitor in a free-roaming \ac{VR} museum from eye tracking, \ac{EDA}, \ac{HRV}, and speech, and what factors limit or improve this prediction?

\medskip
\noindent The primary question decomposes into five subsidiary questions, each addressing one unknown the setting leaves unresolved:

blocks.lead:
% \sloppy here so the long RQ labels stretch the interword spaces rather than
% pushing the last word of a line past the text block

blocks.body: \item[RQ2: Target Representation.] Does expressing the continuous ratings as a small number of ordered levels raise agreement above chance, measured on pooled \ac{QWK} with balanced accuracy against its own chance value as a cross-check, and how many levels does the cohort support?

\item[RQ3: Localisation.] Does restricting prediction to the seconds in which a visitor attends a painting or \ac{AOI}, scored on the same rows as the whole-session model, raise \ac{CCC} and \ac{QWK}?

\item[RQ4: Sources of Shared Variance.] What percentage of the variance in the affect ratings is attributable to the painting attended, to stable differences between visitors, and to residual within-visit variation, and which sensors carry the painting-shared component?
This thesis makes six contributions.

\begin{enumerate}
\item A subject-independent benchmark of valence--arousal prediction in a free-roaming \ac{VR} museum, covering five sensors and two annotation streams, scored entirely leave-one-subject-out.
\item A preprocessing and feature pipeline in which every parameter the literature leaves open is selected empirically under the evaluation protocol, rather than assumed.
\item A comparison of continuous and ordinal target representations, evaluated on identical rows.
\item A test of whether scoping prediction to the attended painting recovers structure a whole-session model misses.
\item A crossed mixed-effects decomposition of affect into visitor, painting, and residual variance, extended to each sensor's own features.

\item An evaluation of three personalisation strategies, tested visitor by visitor.
\end{enumerate}
Each design decision depends on the one before it: how affect is represented constrains how it can be annotated, and how it is annotated constrains what a sensor can be asked to predict.

blocks.lead:
\section{Dimensional Models of Affect and the Annotation Problem}
\label{sec:dimensional-models}

blocks.body: Emotion can be represented either as a set of discrete categories or as a position along continuous dimensions. Discrete models sort feelings into fixed classes such as ``happy'' or ``sad''. Russell's circumplex model instead places affect on two continuous axes: \textbf{Valence}, running from unpleasant to pleasant, and \textbf{Arousal}, from calm to excited \citep{Russell1980} (Figure~\ref{fig:circumplex}). Any state is then a point in that plane rather than a member of a class. That is what lets a rating move gradually as an experience unfolds instead of jumping between labels.

Measuring those axes is easier than obtaining a ground truth for them. Affect is not externally visible in the way a movement or a gaze direction is, so the value has to come from the person feeling it. Reporting takes time. Outside the laboratory reporting becomes harder still: collecting and annotating affect in the wild is named among the field's main open problems, and arousal in particular is a concept untrained raters find unfamiliar \citep{Larradet2020Wild}. Two families of method divide on when that reporting happens. \ac{RCEA} has the person rate their state while the experience is still running, moving a joystick over the same two-axis plane \citep{XueRCEA2021}. This places the rating in the moment, but pays for it in delay. Roughly one to three seconds separate the onset of a feeling from the act of recording it \citep{Mariooryad2015}. A sensor reading and the rating meant to explain it are therefore never quite aligned. RetroSketch instead has the person rate afterwards, from a replay of their own session, which removes that delay but makes the rating depend on what they remember.

The two do not simply substitute for one another. A comparison of retrospective sketching against experience sampling in \ac{VR} found the two highly correlated, but the retrospective method captured a wider range of reported emotion \citep{Potts2025}. Where real-time and retrospective ratings have been collected from the same visitors on the same axes, they were found not to converge on a single shared ground truth \citep{vanderKaaden2026}. Neither can therefore be treated as a corrected version of the other. The annotations analysed in this thesis were collected by both methods, each recorded on the circumplex axes of Figure~\ref{fig:circumplex}, and the two streams are carried separately throughout.

blocks.lead:
\section{Ordinal Targets and the Discretisation of Continuous Affect}
\label{sec:ordinal-lit}

blocks.body: Much emotion-recognition work discretises valence and arousal before predicting them, commonly into a binary high/low split on each axis. Accuracy is then reported against those classes rather than as agreement with the original trace. Two widely used benchmarks follow this pattern: DEAP splits its nine-point valence and arousal ratings at the scale midpoint \citep{Koelstra2012}, while MAHNOB-HCI derives a small number of ordered classes from its self-report \citep{Soleymani2012}.

Where levels are used, they are treated as ordered, not as independent categories. Affect is argued to be ordinal by nature, since people judge emotional states against reference points instead of on an absolute scale. Treating annotation traces this way ``not only yields more valid but also more general models of affect'' \citep{Yannakakis2018}. The practical difficulty is that the same number need not mean the same thing for two people. One visitor's 9 may be another's 7, because each judges against their own recent experience rather than a fixed external standard. The ordering survives that difference, since both agree that the moment was more pleasant than the one before it.

In text emotion prediction, where emotion words are ordered along valence and arousal, ``not all misclassifications are of the same importance, as there are perceptual similarities among emotional classes'' \citep{Mitsios2024}. An ordinal treatment there preserved accuracy while substantially reducing the size of the errors that remained. Scoring such a target therefore needs a measure of how far a prediction falls from the truth, not merely of whether it is right or wrong. \ac{QWK} \citep{Cohen1968} weights each disagreement by the square of the distance between the true and predicted levels. It is the measure most commonly used to summarise agreement on ordered categories. Its value is sensitive, though, to the range of scores used and to how unevenly the classes are filled, which is reason to avoid relying on it alone \citep{Doewes2023}.

The ordinal form is strongest on unbounded labels, where it achieves the highest \ac{CCC} \citep{WuOrdinal2025}. On bounded scales its advantage shows instead in how faithfully relative change is tracked. Discretising a bounded rating is therefore not, in itself, expected to improve agreement with the original trace. Dividing a continuous scale also costs something. A reading close to a level boundary is assigned wholly to one side of it, so the information that it was borderline is lost. Equal-width levels also assume that each step feels the same size to the person rating, which need not hold on a subjective scale. Findings on how many levels to use disagree, and the largest comparison of response granularity reports reliability rising as the scale gets finer rather than peaking at some middling count \citep{Yang2026}. The finer the division, the fewer readings each level receives.

Wearable, minimally intrusive sensors are the standard instrumentation for affect recognition in both laboratory and field studies \citep{Schmidt2019Wearable}. Eye movements index emotional and cognitive state \citep{Adhanom2023}. Pupil size grows with arousal, dilating to both pleasant and unpleasant stimuli relative to neutral ones \citep{Partala2003}. Fixation duration and saccade rate track self-reported anxiety \citep{Adhanom2023}. Eye tracking runs at a high sampling rate and captures brief events that slower sensors miss. Gaze, though, is driven by what is displayed as well as by the viewer's state. Eye features support continuous valence--arousal prediction directly \citep{ODwyer2019}. A network that concatenates the temporal dynamics of those features with the usual summary statistics classifies valence and arousal levels more accurately than earlier eye-tracking models \citep{Gu2025TemporalCapsule}. The closest precedent comes from \ac{VR} itself. Models were trained on pupil reactivity and gaze from 105 participants viewing emotional images in a headset \citep{Szymanska2025}. On a binary high/low split they reached F1 scores of $0.73$ for arousal and $0.64$ for valence. Classifying the same signals into nine levels dropped these to $0.31$ and $0.28$. Coarse pupil-based prediction in \ac{VR} is therefore feasible, but accuracy falls sharply as the target is refined. The images came from standard emotional-picture databases, and the binary split contrasted only extreme ratings. The setting was seated viewing of static images, not free-roaming.

\ac{EDA} reflects sweat-gland activity governed by the sympathetic nervous system \citep{Boucsein2012, Kreibig2010}, and can be recorded without clinical equipment. It is only one facet of the physiological response, however. The field has moved towards wearable systems that pair it with heart rate and other signals \citep{Gedam2025BeyondEDA}. The signal is decomposed into a slow tonic level and fast phasic skin-conductance responses (SCRs). A convex-optimisation formulation recovers both components without resorting to a filter split \citep{Greco2016}. The signal works outside the laboratory, separating three levels of driver stress during real-world driving \citep{Healey2005}. The signal is slow, however. The phasic impulse lasts under two seconds, but the measured response rises and decays over several more \citep{BenedekDeconv2010}. It also degrades under movement \citep{vanderKaaden2026}.

\ac{PPG} yields inter-beat intervals, from which \ac{HRV} indices are computed. These fall into three families: time-domain measures of interval variability, frequency-domain band powers, and nonlinear measures, among them the indices derived from the Poincar\'e plot \citep{Shaffer2017}. How valence appears in cardiac activity depends on arousal. Its signature in brain--heart coupling is clearest at intermediate arousal and is dampened as arousal rises \citep{Valenza2014}. Like \ac{EDA}, \ac{PPG} suffers from movement noise and from poor contact at the wrist \citep{vanderKaaden2026}.

Speech carries affect in how it is spoken. The GeMAPS descriptor set captures these cues in 62 parameters, with an 88-parameter extension, kept small to guard against over-fitting \citep{Eyben2016}. Self-supervised embeddings such as wav2vec2 and WavLM perform better across speech tasks, emotion recognition among them \citep{Baevski2020, Chen2022WavLM, Yang2021}. They are pre-trained on tens of thousands of hours of unlabelled audio, far more than any affect study collects. The representation is therefore fixed before the affect data is seen. What is said also carries affect, and lexicon-based scoring provides a training-free estimate of valence per utterance \citep{Hutto2014} once speech has been transcribed automatically \citep{Radford2022}.
The word ``alignment'' covers three different problems, and treating them as one causes confusion.

\textbf{Device-clock synchronisation} puts sensors that each keep their own clock onto one shared timeline. If both devices record the same kind of signal, sliding one against the other until they best match recovers the offset between their clocks.

\textbf{Label-lag alignment} lines up the sensor timeline with the self-report timeline. A rating takes time to produce, so the feature window that best explains it may sit before, after, or across the moment it was recorded. An early continuous-affect pipeline handled this by shifting the ratings back in time rather than assuming no lag \citep{He2015AVEC}.

\textbf{Representation-level alignment} is the third, and the subject of this section. Two sensors can sit on the same clock and still not correspond in what they show, one responding seconds after the other or over a longer stretch of time. The question is whether matching their dynamics needs a method learned from the data, or whether placing both in the same fixed window is enough.

The three are not equally settled. Clock synchronisation has established solutions. Label-lag has no settled solution, because the correction depends on estimates that vary by annotator, dimension and stimulus. Representation-level alignment is unsettled in a different way: several methods exist, and they differ in what they assume about the signals.

Sensors also sample at very different rates. Pairing their windows naively then degrades the relationship between them. At a 30:1 ratio, such as 120\,Hz eye tracking against 4\,Hz \ac{EDA}, hundreds of gaze samples are tied to a handful of electrodermal readings. How well a fused model performs depends on how that gap is handled \citep{Kumar2025}.
Four methods are relevant. They differ in how much they learn from the data, and in whether they adjust timing at all.

\textbf{Fixed temporal windowing} cuts every signal into windows of the same length and summarises each with a few statistics, such as its mean and spread. Nothing is learned from the data. Averaging also loses the order of events inside a window: a fixation followed two seconds later by a rise in skin conductance looks the same as the two happening at once.

\textbf{\ac{DTW}} \citep{Sakoe1978} stretches and compresses one signal's timeline until it best matches the other, leaving the feature values untouched. It returns not the warped signal but a single number: the distance still separating the two patterns once timing differences are removed, normalised by the length of the path that achieved it. That number was proposed as a recognition score, and the original work finds it discriminates best when the warping is held under a slope constraint rather than left free.

\textbf{\ac{DCTW}} \citep{Trigeorgis2016} learns new features and a warping of the timeline jointly, so that the transformed signals are both maximally correlated and temporally aligned. The two halves are solved by alternating between them rather than in one step.

\textbf{\ac{DCCA}} \citep{Andrew2013} learns such features too, but performs no warping: it is the special case of \ac{DCTW} with the warping fixed to the identity. It requires the two views to arrive as paired observations, one column of each matched to one of the other, since its objective is built on the cross-covariance between them. The original work obtains that pairing by downsampling the faster view. It is also defined for two views only.

Fixed windowing is therefore the baseline the other three are measured against. How much data the learned methods need is a question about sequence length rather than about cohort size. The original \ac{DCTW} experiments align sequences of several thousand samples with a fixed three-layer network, a topology its authors chose to limit overfitting at that scale. They evaluate it on the same sequences it is fitted to rather than on held-out ones.

blocks.lead:
\section{Modelling and Fusion for Small Multimodal Data}
\label{sec:fusion-strategy}

blocks.body: Four questions govern how a small multimodal cohort should be modelled: what a cohort of this size can support, which model families suit it, how the sensors are combined once chosen, and whether the relationship between two sensors is itself worth measuring.

A systematic review of wearable emotion recognition in everyday life, screening over 3,000 studies, finds the evidence base still dominated by laboratory elicitation and names large-scale work in the wild among the field's main open problems \citep{Saganowski2022Everyday}. Across nineteen physiological affect datasets, scored on participants held out of training, handcrafted features generalise to new people better than deep networks trained on raw signal \citep{FEEL2025}. That evidence concerns networks trained from scratch. Two further lines of work approach the same shortage of data from other directions. Pretrained foundation models for physiological signals supply a general-purpose embedding learned from large external corpora rather than from the participants of any one study \citep{Luo2024NormWear}. Self-supervised contrastive learning is the second: representations learned from unlabelled wearable signal outperformed eight self-supervised alternatives on seven of twelve leave-one-subject-out tasks, and stayed more robust when parts of the signal were lost \citep{SigRep2022}.

Among network architectures for a signal sampled over time, two families are established. Recurrence carries a state forward step by step; convolution slides a shared filter along the sequence. Across eleven sequence benchmarks, a simple convolutional architecture outperformed canonical recurrent networks such as \ac{LSTM} on most, and held a longer effective memory \citep{Bai2018TCN}. Convolution is also the lighter of the two. It encodes temporal order through weight sharing rather than recurrent state, so its parameter count follows kernel width and channel count, not sequence length. Dilated convolution, which spaces the filter taps apart, extends the span a given depth can see without adding parameters in proportion. For classifying whole time series, a plain stack of convolutional blocks ending in global average pooling, with no fully connected layers, was proposed as a simple but strong baseline \citep{Wang2017FCN}. A later benchmark of nine deep architectures over the 85 datasets of the standard archive established it as one: that baseline and a residual network were the two strongest of the nine, the residual network significantly ahead of it \citep{IsmailFawaz2019}.

\textbf{Tree-based ensembles} remain the stronger family on tabular features of the size studied here, outperforming deep networks across forty-five datasets truncated to ten thousand training samples each; the same work reports the gap narrowing as the training set grows. Heterogeneous features, small samples and extreme values are the characteristics it names as making tabular data hard for a network to exploit \citep{Grinsztajn2022}. \ac{GBT} is realised as XGBoost \citep{Chen2016XGBoost} or LightGBM \citep{Ke2017}. These, alongside a regularised linear model, are the families most often reported for tabular targets.

Where several sensors are available, the first choice is where to join them. \textbf{Early fusion} concatenates features into one model's input; \textbf{late fusion} combines a base model per modality at the prediction level; and \textbf{model-level fusion} couples the modalities inside the model itself, shaped to the application \citep{Poria2017}. A recent survey adds transformer-based architectures and multimodal representation learning as the field's emerging direction \citep{Kumar2025}.

Two sensors can also be combined by measuring how they move relative to one another, and handing that measurement to the model as a feature in its own right. Such a feature describes something neither sensor shows alone: not what the pupil did or what the skin did, but whether the two moved together. CorrNet builds exactly such features. It takes the cross-covariance of two physiological modalities and projects both into a shared space where they correlate as strongly as possible. The projected pair is then used alongside the features computed inside each modality. On subject-independent binary valence and arousal it reaches $76.4\%$ and $74.0\%$ on a seated desktop dataset \citep{Zhang2020CorrNet}. On a mobile one, recorded with a wristband and a wearable eye tracker, it reaches $70.3\%$ and $68.2\%$.

Such features are sensitive to how they are computed. A multiverse analysis of windowed cross-correlation recomputed the same recordings under fifteen combinations of window length and overlap, measuring cardiac synchrony between pairs of people rather than between sensors within one person. Window length alone shifted the magnitude of the estimated synchrony, its dispersion, and in one index the direction of the effect being tested, with the shortest windows inflating the magnitude. The authors recommend choosing a window as a multiple of the duration of the event being measured rather than by convention \citep{Multiverse2025}. The reference level for a measure of this kind is also not zero but a surrogate baseline, because these methods return apparent coupling even between series that were never coupled, and the available surrogate schemes differ in how conservative they are \citep{Moulder2018}. Their demonstrations use between-person motion and video data rather than within-person cross-sensor signals, so what carries over is the need for a surrogate rather than the choice of any particular one.

Which pairs to measure is less settled than whether to measure at all. Heart rate, electrodermal activity, pupil size, head velocity and body movement were recorded concurrently in 37 infants. Heart rate moved with movement across every analysis, and tonic pupil size co-varied positively with the other indices. Electrodermal activity co-varied with none of them at the tonic level, its agreement appearing only phasically and only where arousal was already high \citep{Wass2015}. The cohort is infants, so the finding transfers as a caution rather than as a parameter. It still leaves a tonic pairing built on electrodermal activity with the least prior support of those available. The pupil and electrodermal pairing, in contrast, has direct support: pupillary change during affective picture viewing co-varies with skin conductance change, and both are read as indices of sympathetic activation \citep{Bradley2008}. That co-variation is measured across pictures in a seated, dim-room viewing task, so it establishes that the two respond to the same affective material rather than that they track one another second by second in a moving visitor. A separate family of measures, built on the same modality pairs, quantifies synchrony between people rather than between sensors within one person \citep{GroupSynchrony2023}. The two answer different questions.

\section{The HERE Dataset and What Its Analysis Showed}
\label{sec:bas-findings}

blocks.body: Exploratory data analysis is the standard first step with a recorded dataset: displays of the data suggest hypotheses, and each hypothesis is tested against the data before any confirmatory step \citep{Tukey1977}. Completeness, accuracy and consistency are among the dimensions the data-quality literature checks a dataset against \citep{Batini2009}.

Van der Kaaden \citep{vanderKaaden2026} collected multimodal data from forty-five visitors, twenty-two assigned to real-time and twenty-three to retrospective annotation. His preprocessing used pulse-peak detection for \ac{HRV} from \ac{PPG}. \ac{EDA} was bandpassed at 0.01--5\,Hz, corrected for motion artefacts, and decomposed into tonic and phasic parts with NeuroKit2 \citep{Makowski2021}. Eye tracking went through standard pupillometry \citep{Kret2019}, and push-to-talk speech through prosodic extraction. Features are extracted over fixed windows sized from published response latencies and resampled to the annotation rate (trailing 60\,s for \ac{HRV}, 12\,s for \ac{EDA}, 8\,s for pupil). He notes that window-based extraction collapses high-frequency dynamics into summary statistics, and that the 1\,Hz annotation rate sets a temporal ceiling below which finer variation is not recoverable \citep{vanderKaaden2026}.

For the real-time stream he estimated the annotator's reporting delay four independent ways. He marked stimulus moments by hand in practice videos. He detected peaks in the features. He searched for the delay that best correlated candidate features with the annotation. He then took whichever delay gave the best classification result. None converged on a stable estimate. He resolved it from the general trend across the four, read alongside reaction-lag figures from comparable continuous-annotation benchmarks. The applied correction is fixed and asymmetric, one second for arousal and two for valence, since arousal is reported faster. A robustness check found no meaningful difference in feature-annotation correlations between the corrected and unshifted annotations.

He also modelled the data, aligning all modalities to a 1\,Hz timeline and discretising the valence--arousal space into seven $k$-means regions. Four classifiers were compared: a random forest, extra trees, a radial-basis support-vector machine, and logistic regression. Each ran under both within-participant and \ac{LOSO} cross-validation, on roughly 2,500 real-time and 1,200 retrospective rows. Five findings stand out:

\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Learns within a person, not across people.} Trained and tested on the same people, the model classified affect well, at ${\approx}0.84$ balanced accuracy. On a new person it fell close to chance: ${\approx}0.20$--$0.24$ for the tree models he emphasised, and as low as ${\approx}0.10$ for the simplest. A model trained on one annotation method barely worked on the other (${\approx}0.17$--$0.18$). Across his forty-five visitors the patterns the classifier recovered were therefore individual rather than shared.
  \item \textbf{Sensors barely track self-report.} Correlations between the annotations and the features were weak (speech and text $|r|\!\leq\!0.11$, physiology $|r|\!\leq\!0.07$). He attributes the weak correlations to museum affect that changes slowly and to time-windowed smoothing that removes brief physiological spikes.
  \item \textbf{Visitors do not agree.} Looking at the same painting, visitors did not report the same emotion (inter-rater \ac{ICC} near zero, the highest $0.064$): the response came from the person, not the picture.
  \item \textbf{Two different ground truths.} \ac{RCEA} (real-time) is sparse and step-like, mostly sitting at a neutral baseline with occasional jumps; RetroSketch (rated from a replay afterwards) is smoother and covers more of the range, but is shaped by what the visitor remembers. RetroSketch covers more of the affect space per person, while \ac{RCEA} leaves gaps. He concludes that the two do not converge on a single shared ground truth; each represents the same experience differently. Keeping them separate throughout this thesis is a choice built on that finding, not one he draws himself.
  \item \textbf{Same experience, different cost.} Workload, presence and cybersickness did not differ between the methods. RetroSketch took considerably longer, however, since visitors re-watched and annotated the whole session afterwards, and their time in \ac{VR} was correspondingly shorter.
\end{itemize}

Whether one person's affect can be predicted is separate from whether different people react alike. Naturalistic neuroscience measures the latter three ways. Intersubject correlation \citep{Hasson2004, Nastase2019} and the \ac{ICC} \citep{Shrout1979, Koo2016} measure agreement directly. Mixed models instead split the total variation into what the stimulus drives and what the person drives. The person-specific part of a naturalistic response has been shown to be reliable rather than noise \citep{Finn2020}, so telling shared variation apart from person-specific variation is informative in itself. The same tools have been applied to aesthetic ratings, where individual differences are large. On audio-aesthetic ratings of singing voices, inter-rater agreement was low even where average preferences were stable across cohorts \citep{Bruder2024}. Splitting the total variation into a stimulus share and a person share, rather than reporting how far raters agree, asks a different question of the same data.

This pattern holds beyond ratings alone. \ac{EDA} and heart rate can align across people given the same content, often because they attend to the same moments \citep{Stuldreher2020}, and the same alignment has been measured with wearable sensors \citep{Stuldreher2023}. Responses to art, however, are only partly shared \citep{Specker2020}. A sound analysis treats the participant as the unit and separates within- from between-person variation \citep{Aarts2014}, and corrects for multiple tests \citep{Benjamini1995}. Where responses are neither fully shared nor fully personal, describing recurring response types has improved cross-person recognition \citep{GutierrezMartin2024}.

If the affective response is largely person-specific, the standard response is to adapt the model to the individual; per-user calibration has been reported to lift cross-person accuracy \citep{Abinaya2026}. The methods that implement it differ chiefly in what they ask of the new person.

The cheapest ask nothing but the new person's unlabelled signal. Physiological baselines differ between people for reasons unrelated to affect, so a raw sensor value is not comparable across visitors. Removing each person's own resting level before prediction addresses exactly that. Distribution alignment generalises the same idea beyond a simple offset. Correlation alignment (CORAL) rescales the training features so that their spread and correlations match the new person's, using only that person's unlabelled data and no repeated training \citep{SunSaenko2016CORAL}. Methods of this family are called domain adaptation, in contrast with domain generalisation, which learns features that hold across many people without seeing the new person.

More is available if the new person can be asked for labels. Few-shot fine-tuning adapts a population model on a small annotated sample from the target. Combined with distribution alignment, it reached $93.4\%$ and $82.3\%$ on two established \ac{EEG} benchmarks, though on categorical rather than dimensional targets \citep{Lu2023DFFNet}.

Two cautions follow. First, the reported successes come overwhelmingly from \ac{EEG} in the laboratory. There the emotion is deliberately provoked, the contrast between states is strong, and the signal comes from the head rather than the wrist; one systematic review excluded \ac{EEG} studies outright as usable only in stationary settings \citep{Saganowski2022Everyday}. Accuracies obtained that way are a poor guide to what wrist and eye sensors can support during free movement. Second, there is no guarantee that transferability is uniform across the two axes, so a result on one axis should not be assumed to hold on the other. Across nineteen physiological affect datasets, models are accordingly scored on people held out of training, with high inter-subject variability a named challenge \citep{FEEL2025}.

A fourth approach adapts the target instead. Each person uses a rating scale with their own central tendency and spread, so a fixed cohort-wide threshold does not mean the same thing for two visitors. Per-person standardisation removes that difference: on a discretised target, each person's level boundaries come from their own ratings, not fixed across the cohort. Outside these families, subject-invariant features can be learned by aligning people contrastively \citep{Shen2023CLISA}, or person-specific structure retrieved from the person's own history instead of modelled \citep{Simon2026RAP}.

Five experiments, run on one cohort under one protocol, answer the research questions of Section~\ref{sec:research-questions}. The five build on one another, each settling a choice the next depends on, so they appear in the order they run. Experiment~1 settles each sensor's searched configuration and the standard prediction model. Experiment~2 settles how the sensors are combined. Experiment~3 settles the target representation and its level count, decided independently for each condition and axis. Experiment~4 scopes prediction to the seconds a visitor attends a painting and bounds what any model could recover, through a variance decomposition of the ratings. Experiment~5 tests adaptation to the individual visitor and carries nothing further forward. The protocol every experiment shares and the data itself come first, in Sections~\ref{sec:protocol} and~\ref{sec:methodology-characterization}; Appendix~\ref{app:alt-supplementary} summarises the configuration each component of the pipeline ends up carrying.

\textbf{Data.} This thesis analyses a free-roaming visit to a \ac{VR} museum exhibition: worn eye-tracking, skin-conductance, heart-rate, and speech sensors, alongside two self-report annotation streams. Visitors stopped to look at five paintings along the way (B1, B2, B3, C5, C6; Figure~\ref{fig:stimuli}), the stimuli every later experiment ties sensor rows to. Three auxiliary channels sit beside the sensors and are never predicted from. The wristband also records acceleration and skin temperature: acceleration drives the electrodermal motion mask, and temperature is kept as a reference against which the tonic electrodermal level is read (Section~\ref{sec:results-characterization-alt}). The \ac{VR} engine keeps a gaze-and-behaviour log carrying the visitor's floor position, which drives teleport detection and the attended-painting definition of Experiment~4. \ac{RCEA} was collected continuously and in real time during the visit; RetroSketch was collected retrospectively from a replay of the session. The two streams capture affect in structurally different ways, so a model trained on one is not assumed to transfer to the other; this thesis reports the two conditions separately throughout and never pools them.

\textbf{Continuous prediction as the starting point.} The most direct reading of ``recover a visitor's valence and arousal'' is to predict the continuous $0$--$10$ ratings themselves. Two considerations argue against this as the final target. These self-ratings are person-relative, with no shared scale or common zero: one visitor's ``6'' for arousal need not mean what another's does. What counts as a given emotion also differs from person to person \citep{Barrett2006}. Continuous labels also carry annotator-specific reaction lags, varying by annotator and by dimension, that would have to be modelled out before two visitors' ratings could be compared on the same footing \citep{Mariooryad2015}. Every experiment from Experiment~3 onward therefore works with a discretised, per-axis target instead. This changes the prediction task, not only the target: Experiments~1 and~2 are regression problems, fitted and scored on the continuous rating, while Experiments~3 to~5 are ordinal multiclass classification problems with $B$ ordered levels per axis. The continuous target is kept for the first two deliberately: a continuous score separates candidate pipelines more finely than a handful of levels, so each sensor's representation and model can be chosen cleanly before any level boundary enters.

\textbf{Evaluation protocol.} Throughout this thesis, a slice is one annotation stream crossed with one axis: valence and arousal on rcea and retro give four slices, and every score is computed and reported per slice. Every experiment is scored under leave-one-subject-out cross-validation (\ac{LOSO}): a model is trained on all but one visitor and tested on the one held out, repeated until every visitor has been held out. Each slice carries one fold per visitor with usable annotation; usability is established by the coverage audit of Section~\ref{sec:methodology-characterization}, and the resulting participant and fold counts are reported in Section~\ref{sec:results-characterization-alt}.

Continuous predictions are scored by the \ac{CCC}. Ordinal predictions, from the classifier fitted on the binned target (Section~\ref{sec:methodology-binning-alt}), are scored by pooled \ac{QWK} and balanced accuracy together. \ac{QWK} \citep{Cohen1968} weights a disagreement by the square of the distance between the true and predicted levels, and is the headline figure. Balanced accuracy, the mean per-level recall, is the cross-check, read against its chance value of $1/B$. A pooled score is computed once over the held-out predictions of all folds taken together, instead of averaging one score per fold. For both \ac{CCC} and \ac{QWK}, zero is the value expected of a model carrying no usable information about the held-out visitor, and both can fall below it; this zero is what the results chapter calls the chance-corrected floor.

\textbf{Missing feature values.} A feature can be absent for a given second because its sensor was not usable then, and the speech features are absent whenever the visitor is not talking, so missingness is routine rather than exceptional (Section~\ref{sec:results-characterization-alt}). Wherever a model is trained on features, a missing value is filled with the median of that feature computed inside the training fold of the current split and applied unchanged to the held-out visitor, so nothing about the test participant reaches the imputer. Every model whose fitting involves randomness is seeded from one fixed value, so a re-run reproduces the numbers reported here; the support-vector regressor is deterministic and takes no seed. The imputer is fitted in the same pipeline as the scaler and the model, refitted for every fold. Imputation is applied to every model family alike, including the boosted trees that could handle missing values natively. All eight families therefore see identical inputs, and a difference between models stays a difference between models. Rows are never dropped for a missing feature. Late fusion needs its own rule, because it combines predictions rather than features. Where a sensor produces no prediction for a row, an averaging rule renormalises its weights over the sensors that did. Every arm is therefore scored on the same rows: every second with a valid annotation for the slice, not only the smaller set where all five sensors happen to be usable at once (Section~\ref{sec:methodology-fusion-alt}).

\textbf{Statistical testing.} Two decision rules are fixed \emph{a priori} to guard against post-hoc selection bias. The first determines whether an observed difference is statistically significant. It is assessed by a Wilcoxon signed-rank test over per-participant scores \citep{Demscar2006}, with the false-discovery rate controlled across each family of hypotheses \citep{Benjamini1995}, and it takes two forms. Experiment~1 applies it as a single-sample test, asking whether each feature's within-visitor correlation differs from zero, across 436 features at once. Experiments~4 and~5 apply it paired within participant, and there a difference is credited only where it survives correction on both evaluation metrics, which precludes selective reporting.

\textbf{Selection among candidates.} The second rule resolves practical equivalence, and it applies wherever no difference between candidates is significant. Retraining the identical pipeline on identical data yields minor fluctuations in score, and a difference inside that noise floor cannot separate two candidates; the margin below which they are treated as equivalent is the selection resolution. To avoid circularity it is not calibrated on any model the comparisons go on to select, but on one invariant reference cell: the cardiac features against rcea arousal under the starting configuration of Section~\ref{sec:config-selection}. That cell is evaluated twenty times, varying only the pseudo-random seed and the fold-level resampling of training participants, and the margin is the gap between the fifth and ninety-fifth percentiles of the twenty means, rounded up. Because the two metric scales differ, it is estimated separately for \ac{CCC}, which Experiments~1 and~2 are scored on, and for pooled \ac{QWK}, which Experiments~3 to~5 are scored on (Section~\ref{sec:results-unimodal-alt}).

\textbf{Coverage and usability audit.} Coverage is measured on the raw recordings, before any cleaning, artefact rejection, or feature extraction: per sensor and per participant, each second of that participant's analysed window is counted as covered when the raw sensor produced at least one sample within it.

\textbf{Signal quality.} What the coverage audit counts as present is then examined for whether it is usable \citep{Tukey1977}. Sampling rates, timestamps, value ranges and completeness are each verified against what the instrument should have produced, so that no later result rests on a channel that was mislabelled, misaligned in time, or silently empty. The annotation streams are inspected on the same pass, since where a rating rests when untouched bears on the level boundaries of Experiment~3.

\textbf{Visiting behaviour.} The \ac{VR} engine records a gaze-and-behaviour log for every visitor, the same log Experiment~4 later resolves into attended-painting intervals (Section~\ref{sec:methodology-localisation-alt}). Here it is instead put to a lighter, descriptive use, independent of any affect modelling: which painting each visitor viewed first and the order paintings were visited in, how that order compares to the room's physical layout, how long each visitor dwelled at each painting, how often a visitor returned to a painting already seen, and how much a visitor engaged the in-\ac{VR} guide, by message count.

This experiment measures how much of a visitor's valence and arousal each sensor can recover on its own. Five sensors are evaluated on two axes and two annotation streams, and every combination is evaluated independently. Two of the five come from the one speech recording: the acoustics carry how something is said, the content carries what is said, and the two cannot be combined into one representation, so they are counted separately.

\textbf{Pupil and gaze.} The eye tracker reports a pupil diameter and a gaze direction at a nominal rate of 120\,Hz, and both signals require cleaning before use. Samples that the tracker itself flags as invalid are discarded, together with diameters outside the physiologically plausible range of 1.5--9.0\,mm, following the standard preprocessing guideline for pupil data \citep{Kret2019}. The two eyes are then averaged into a single diameter. A blink interrupts the signal and leaves a short gap in the record. Gaps shorter than $0.5$\,s are bridged by linear interpolation, $0.5$\,s being the default blink ceiling in the pupillometry methods literature \citep{Mathot2022Methods}, while longer gaps are left missing; blinks themselves are counted from the tracker's validity flags rather than from gaps. Because the diameter also drifts over the visit, a rolling 30-second mean is subtracted from it; subtracting a baseline rather than dividing by one is the standard treatment \citep{Mathot2018}, taken over a rolling window here since a free visit has no trials to lock a baseline to. The gaze direction carries sample-to-sample noise, so the direction vectors are smoothed with a 5-sample centred median before angular velocity is computed from them, following the noise-reduction step of the Tobii I-VT filter \citep{Olsen2012IVT}, which specifies it for two-dimensional gaze coordinates rather than the three-dimensional direction vectors used here. Velocity is never computed across a gap: sample pairs more than $100$\,ms apart are excluded. Each sample is then classified as belonging to a fixation or a saccade. The classification rule is itself one of the searched parameters (Section~\ref{sec:config-selection}). Two properties of the recording need separate handling. First, the tracker reports the gaze vector in the headset's own reference frame, so locomotion, including teleportation, does not move the vector by itself. A teleport still contaminates the record, because the eyes reflexively re-orient to the new scene, which is an eye movement but not viewing behaviour, and because the abrupt change in luminance moves the pupil. Samples adjacent to a detected teleport are therefore excluded from classification. Teleports are detected from the engine's own position records: a movement faster than $3$\,m/s between neighbouring records is faster than any walk and marks a jump, and a gap in the records is masked as a whole when its endpoints lie further apart than walking pace, $1.5$\,m/s, could cover in the time. Both speeds are chosen here rather than taken from a source; how cleanly they separate walking from teleporting is reported in Section~\ref{sec:results-characterization-alt}. Second, scene luminance affects the pupil throughout the visit, and the pupillography standards ask for luminance to be reported or controlled \citep{Kelbsch2019}. Because this dataset contains no luminance channel, that confound can only be stated, not removed.

\textbf{Electrodermal activity.} Electrodermal activity reflects sympathetic activation through changes in skin conductance, and at the wrist it is fragile in two ways: the electrodes can lose contact, and arm movement disturbs the signal. A recording made without proper skin contact still contains numbers, so two checks remove such recordings first. A recording in which at least half of the samples are negative is removed, because a conductance cannot be negative. A recording whose values stay nearly flat over the visit, spanning less than $0.02$\,\textmu S between their 5th and 95th percentiles, is removed as well, because the smallest deflection that counts as a skin-conductance response is conventionally $0.01$ to $0.05$\,\textmu S \citep{BenedekDeconv2010}. Motion is handled next, using the accelerometer. The acceleration magnitude, smoothed over one second so that a brief jolt registers as one event rather than as scattered samples, is compared against the recording's own median plus a multiple of its median absolute deviation; samples above that threshold are marked contaminated and interpolated over, and the multiplier is one of the searched parameters (Section~\ref{sec:config-selection}). The cleaned signal is then decomposed into a slow tonic level and fast phasic responses, and because no decomposition method is universally preferred, the method is itself searched (Section~\ref{sec:config-selection}). Skin-conductance responses are detected on the phasic component and reported according to the Society for Psychophysiological Research's committee standard \citep{BoucseinSPR2012}. The detector discards a candidate response whose amplitude falls below $0.1$ of the largest phasic amplitude in the same recording, so the threshold scales with each visitor's own signal and holds a quiet recording to a lower absolute bar than an active one. It is a different quantity from the conventional minimum that governs the exclusion rule: that figure is an absolute floor in microsiemens for what counts as a response at all, whereas this one is a proportion of a single recording's own maximum. The value is inherited from the pipeline this dataset originates from, and the range $0.02$ to $0.2$ is swept so that the detected response counts are read against the choice rather than assumed independent of it. One limitation is inherent to the recording site. Wrist-to-palm agreement is $r=0.31$ for the tonic level and $r=0.42$ for the response rate \citep{vanderMee2021}, and a comparison of four recording sites, none of them the wrist, favours the finger and the foot for signal quality and finds the forehead the most robust to motion \citep{Bhatti2022}; since the wrist is what this dataset provides, its \ac{EDA} is read with that limit in mind.

\textbf{Heart-rate variability.} Heart-rate variability quantifies the variation in timing between consecutive heartbeats, and in this dataset it is derived from wrist photoplethysmography. Beats are located with a dual-moving-average detector, validated at $99.8\%$ sensitivity on fingertip recordings taken at rest and after exercise in hot conditions \citep{Elgendi2013}. Wrist recordings made while walking sit outside that validation, and what an optical sensor yields is strictly pulse-rate variability, a surrogate for \ac{HRV} \citep{Schafer2012, Hinde2025}. The interbeat intervals are cleaned in two steps. First, intervals outside the range a heart can produce, 40--180 beats per minute, are removed. Second, the remaining intervals pass a successive-difference filter: an interval whose difference from its predecessor exceeds a multiple of the rolling spread of such differences, taken over a centred 45-beat window, is removed as well. Removed intervals are then interpolated over in time. The successive-difference principle with a time-varying threshold follows \citep{LipponenTarvainen2019}; the window and the multiplier are set here, and the multiplier is one of the searched parameters (Section~\ref{sec:config-selection}). Motion has no separate mask on this channel, although wearable photoplethysmography commonly uses the accelerometer as a reference for motion-artifact removal \citep{Charlton2022PPG}. Instead, each window carries the fraction of its intervals the filters repaired and the fraction of its seconds the accelerometer marks as high motion, so that a contaminated stretch is visible to the model rather than hidden. All indices are computed after these steps.

\textbf{Speech.} Speech was recorded through a push-to-talk channel, so it exists only while a visitor chose to address the guide. Utterance boundaries are taken from the automatic transcript. For each utterance, acoustic parameters are computed with openSMILE over the extended Geneva standardised acoustic parameter set \citep{Eyben2016}, and content is scored with the VADER sentiment lexicon \citep{Hutto2014}. VADER was validated on short informal text, which is closer to spoken remarks than edited prose is; the transfer to speech remains an assumption that this thesis states rather than tests.

Table~\ref{tab:alt-experiment1-sensors} lists the features each sensor contributes. Each sensor is aligned with the annotation by fixed temporal windowing: the annotation is read on a 1\,Hz grid while every sensor runs at its own rate, and aggregating a sensor over a fixed window expresses both on the same grid. A fixed window is chosen over the other alignment methods of Section~\ref{sec:alignment-lit}, warping and learned projections, because a sensor and its annotation come from the same person on the same clock: all that can separate them is a delay, and the searched direction and delay absorb it (Section~\ref{sec:config-selection}). The pupil window is fixed at eight seconds. Cognitive effects on pupil size emerge about half a second after their trigger and unfold over the following two to three seconds \citep{Mathot2022Methods}, so a complete episode spans roughly three to four seconds. Because triggers in a continuous recording are not controlled and need not coincide with the rated second, eight seconds is enough to hold a full episode even when its trigger falls a few seconds to either side. The length is therefore fixed, and only the window's direction and delay are searched (Section~\ref{sec:config-selection}). The \ac{EDA} window trails the rated second and its length is one of the searched parameters (Section~\ref{sec:config-selection}). The \ac{HRV} window is fixed at sixty seconds, the shortest length at which its indices remain valid \citep{Castaldo2019}, and its direction and delay are searched like the pupil's. Speech is aggregated per utterance, because the utterance is the unit for which the standardised acoustic set is defined \citep{Eyben2016}.

\footnotesize
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{4pt}
\caption{The features each sensor contributes.}

Speech features exist only for the seconds an utterance covers; any sensor's features are missing for a second whose window holds no usable signal.

The sixty-second window restricts which \ac{HRV} indices remain valid. Of 23 common indices, six stay consistent down to one minute \citep{Castaldo2019}; four of the six are used, and the omitted two only restate meanNN and SDNN in heart-rate units. RMSSD is added because even a ten-second record yields a valid value \citep{Laborde2017}, and the low- and very-low-frequency indices are excluded because their bands require at least two and five minutes of record \citep{Shaffer2017}. The interval count, the repaired fraction, and the motion fraction are measures of data quality rather than of \ac{HRV}.

Independently of any model, each feature's relation to each axis is measured directly on the features the configuration search carries forward: Spearman's correlation within each participant, summarised across participants by its median and quartiles. Participants are never pooled into one correlation, because differences between people would masquerade as a relation. A feature counts as related only if its per-participant coefficients differ from zero under a Wilcoxon signed-rank test, with the false-discovery rate controlled over all features, axes, and streams \citep{Benjamini1995}, and directions are read against the expectations of Section~\ref{sec:modalities-lit}. These correlations describe the data and decide nothing downstream: no feature is selected or removed because of them.

Five configuration parameters have no single established value: for each, the literature validates several candidates rather than one. Each is therefore decided on this data, by letting the candidates compete. Each also carries a starting value, used wherever a configuration is needed before the competition has run: the 30 degrees per second fixation rule, the uncorrected diameter, trailing windows at zero delay for pupil and \ac{HRV}, an interbeat multiplier of four, and the NeuroKit decomposition under the five-deviation motion mask with a twelve-second window. These are the values the dataset's origin used, so the search begins from the published configuration rather than from an arbitrary one. The candidate sets and the deciding rule are fixed before the competition, and rcea and retro decide separately (Section~\ref{sec:protocol}).

The competition may never see the visitor being predicted, so it runs on the training participants of each fold alone, exactly as the hyperparameters are tuned. Every training participant scores every candidate by \ac{CCC}, the scores are turned into ranks within that participant, and the candidate with the best average rank wins. Ranks are used instead of raw scores so that one extreme participant cannot decide the outcome alone. Every candidate's mean, median and range are reported, and ties are resolved toward the simpler candidate at the selection resolution of Section~\ref{sec:protocol}. The model that produces those scores is ridge regression, the reference family. It is cheap enough to fit every candidate on every fold, and scoring a configuration with the reference family, rather than with the family the model comparison selects, keeps the configuration from being tuned to that family. A configuration chosen under one model could in principle suit another less well. That is a limitation of the design, and how far it reaches is bounded by the spread of candidate scores, reported in Section~\ref{sec:results-selection-alt}.

When one sensor has several searched parameters, they are decided one at a time, in the order the processing chain runs: for pupil, first the fixation rule, then the gaze-angle correction, then the window direction and delay. Deciding all three at once would mean comparing 112 combinations, and a winner picked from that many options on the training participants of one fold would mostly reflect chance rather than a real difference \citep{Cawley2010}. Deciding one at a time can miss settings that only work in combination, but the pupil steps act on separate parts of the signal, so little is lost: the fixation rule reads the gaze direction, the correction changes only the diameter. The one exception is \ac{EDA}, where the decomposition and the motion mask are decided together, because both shape the detected skin-conductance responses. The \ac{HRV} annotation delay, finally, is not chosen from a list but estimated per participant, again only inside the training fold. That ordering extends to the model families: all five configuration parameters are settled before the eight families are compared. Deciding configuration and family jointly would multiply the candidates in the same way, and the cost is the same one: a configuration that suits the selected family better than it suits the reference family would never be found.

\textbf{Fixation detection.} Four candidate rules are compared, spanning the velocity-threshold, dispersion, and adaptive families \citep{SalvucciGoldberg2000}. A velocity threshold of 30 degrees per second is the default criterion for seated screen-based viewing \citep{Olsen2012IVT}, and one of 240 degrees per second is validated for walking, where the eye's stabilising movements contaminate lower criteria \citep{Stuart2014}. A dispersion rule classifying at 1 degree over 0.25\,s was calibrated on this headset class, though in a stationary task \citep{LlanesJurado2020}. A per-recording adaptive threshold is estimated iteratively from the velocity samples below the current threshold \citep{NystromHolmqvist2010}, and estimating it from median-based statistics instead makes it robust to the saccades it is meant to detect \citep{Voloh2020}.

\textbf{Gaze-angle correction.} Two candidates are compared: correcting the diameter for gaze angle, and leaving it uncorrected. A pupil viewed at an angle is imaged smaller than it is, an error on a par with the task-evoked responses themselves in head-mounted trackers \citep{PeterschDierkes2021}. Gaze position accounts for between $9\%$ and $20\%$ of measured pupil variance, depending on the tracker, and correcting for it is both necessary and achievable \citep{HayesPetrov2015}. The correction used here regresses each participant's diameter on their own gaze direction and keeps the residual; whether it helps in a headset is tested rather than assumed.

\textbf{Window direction and annotation delay.} A sensor and the annotation run on the same clock inside the same person: the body responds to a moment, and the report follows it, so the misalignment between the two is a lag, not a difference in tempo. The annotation is therefore aligned by a rigid shift, never by a warp. A shift is a single shared parameter, applied unchanged to the held-out visitor. A warp is fitted per recording, so the held-out visitor's warp would need that visitor's own ratings, which no part of this pipeline may touch; a warp is also free enough to align almost any two series, so agreement after warping is weak evidence of a real relation. Shifting is the field's own remedy for label lag \citep{He2015AVEC}, and because reaction lag varies by annotator and by dimension \citep{Mariooryad2015}, the shift is searched rather than assumed. For pupil and \ac{HRV} the search compares trailing against forward windows, at delays from zero to six seconds in each direction, and a per-participant estimated delay against a fixed delay; the electrodermal window only trails, because its response begins seconds after its trigger. A held-out visitor, whose own delay cannot be estimated without their ratings, receives the median of the training participants' estimated delays. Experiment~2 requires all five sensors on one label grid, so a per-sensor estimated delay is kept only where it improves \ac{CCC} by more than the selection resolution.

\textbf{Interbeat outlier multiplier.} The candidates are three, four, and five times the rolling spread of successive interval differences. The successive-difference principle is established \citep{LipponenTarvainen2019}; the specific multipliers are set here.

\textbf{Electrodermal decomposition, motion mask and window.} Because a comparison of seven quantification approaches found none universally best \citep{Kuijpers2022}, the decomposition is searched: the frequency split against the convex-optimisation method \citep{Greco2016}. Each is crossed with mask multipliers of two, three, and five median absolute deviations; in free-moving immersive \ac{VR}, automated artefact correction has been shown to match manual expert cleaning at the phasic level \citep{LlanesJurado2021}. The selected configuration is then swept over windows of 3, 6, 8, 12, and 20 seconds. The floor comes from the response itself, whose deconvolved impulse lasts about $1.6$\,s and which begins one to three seconds after its trigger \citep{BenedekDeconv2010}; a seated sweep finding three-second windows best \citep{MercadoDiaz2024} argues for candidates shorter than the twelve seconds previously used on this dataset, and the 20-second window is kept as a deliberately long secondary.

Eight model families are compared: ridge regression, a support-vector regressor with a radial-basis kernel, a random forest, extremely randomised trees, histogram gradient boosting, XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost. The features are tabular and the cohort is small, and on such data tree-based ensembles are the strongest reported family (Section~\ref{sec:fusion-strategy}); ridge is the simple reference the others are read against, and the support-vector regressor is the nonlinear alternative that is not a tree. The four boosting entries are one method under four libraries, so the choice of library cannot decide the result. The pool also contains the four families the dataset's origin used \citep{vanderKaaden2026}.

Each family carries a three-candidate hyperparameter grid, tuned by a nested search inside every training fold, so no tuning decision sees the held-out visitor: candidates are scored on an inner split of the training participants and the winner is refitted on the full fold \citep{Cawley2010}. Ridge, being cheap to fit, tunes on an inner leave-one-subject-out split; the tree, boosting, and kernel families tune on an inner five-fold split grouped by participant, which costs less.

The standard model carried into every later experiment is chosen among the tree ensembles, the class the evidence of Section~\ref{sec:fusion-strategy} supports for tabular features at this sample size, with ridge regression and the support-vector regressor scored alongside as references. The family with the highest mean \ac{CCC} over the twenty sensor-by-slice cells is carried, subject to the selection convention of Section~\ref{sec:protocol}: families within the selection resolution of one another are tied, and a tie is resolved toward the family whose scores vary least across the twenty cells. Families are compared on the mean, the median, the spread and the extremes of those cells together, since a single summary can rank them in orders the others do not support.

This experiment asks whether combining the sensors recovers more of a visitor's valence and arousal than any sensor recovers on its own, and it answers in three steps. The first settles how the sensors' timelines are reconciled onto one shared grid: the four available alignment methods are compared against one another, and the best of them is carried forward. The second builds a small set of columns that measure how two sensors move relative to one another, which is something no sensor shows on its own; they are offered to the third step as an addition to the sensors' own features rather than as a replacement for them. The third compares the mechanisms by which the aligned sensors are actually combined, with and without those columns, so that what they contribute can be read separately. Alignment matters only where features from different sensors enter a single model, so the method decided in the first step governs early fusion alone; late fusion combines one prediction per sensor on the shared label grid, and therefore needs no further alignment.

The five sensors each run at their own native rate before they reach the common 1\,Hz label grid, and the four ways of reconciling them set out in Section~\ref{sec:alignment-lit} are all compared here, on the three physiological pairs: pupil with \ac{EDA}, pupil with \ac{HRV}, and \ac{EDA} with \ac{HRV}.

\textbf{Fixed temporal windowing} is the baseline. Each sensor is aggregated into the window it carries out of Experiment~1, and the resulting features are read off the shared per-stream grid of Section~\ref{sec:protocol}.

\textbf{\ac{DTW}} \citep{Sakoe1978} adds three columns for each pair, nine in all. For a given second, both signals of the pair are read from a common twelve-second trailing window, placed on a shared 4\,Hz grid and standardised, and then warped against one another. The three columns that follow are the distance still separating the two signals once the warp has been applied, the mean signed offset along the warping path, in grid samples of $0.25$\,s, and the extent to which that path departs from the diagonal.

\textbf{\ac{DCCA}} \citep{Andrew2013} adds learned correlated projections of the same three pairs, and \textbf{\ac{DCTW}} \citep{Trigeorgis2016} adds a warping step to those projections. Both are fitted inside each outer training fold, on the training participants alone, and are then applied to the held-out visitor, so that no projection is ever fitted on the visitor whose rows it scores.

All four arms are scored on identical rows, by the standard model held at one fixed configuration, so that what separates them is the alignment method rather than anything downstream of it. The arm with the highest mean \ac{CCC} across the four slices is the one carried into the fusion comparisons that follow, with ties resolved as in Section~\ref{sec:protocol}.

The previous experiment measures each sensor on its own. Nothing in it can tell whether two sensors moved together. This experiment measures it directly instead. The result is a block of columns that is added to the early-fusion feature matrix in one of the arms of Section~\ref{sec:methodology-combination-alt}, so that what the block contributes can be read against the same model run without it.

The columns are built from three signals: the baseline-corrected pupil diameter, the phasic electrodermal component, and the instantaneous heart rate. Each is taken as it runs, not as the per-window summaries Experiment~1 computes from it, because correlating two summaries would measure how the summaries move rather than how the signals do. All three are placed on a shared 4\,Hz grid, since a one-second grid is too coarse for lags searched to five seconds and for responses that unfold over two to three. The three signals make three pairs, and each pair is described in up to three ways: whether the two signals move together, whether they move together once one is allowed to lag the other, and whether an event in one is followed by an event in the other. Table~\ref{tab:alt-crosssensor-columns} lists the eight columns this produces.
