The lag is bounded at five seconds in either direction, and that bound comes from how quickly each system can respond. A pupil response begins about half a second after its trigger and unfolds over the following two to three seconds \citep{Mathot2022Methods}, so it has peaked by about three seconds. An electrodermal response to the same trigger begins one to three seconds after it \citep{BenedekDeconv2010} and takes a further two to three seconds, so it can peak as late as six. The widest separation the two can plausibly show is therefore about three seconds, and five is taken as the bound so that a slower response than these figures describe still falls inside it. A single coupled episode lasts roughly three to five seconds on the same arithmetic.

The event columns count only the skin-conductance responses that begin after a pupil dilation. The electrodermal system is the slower of the two and cannot respond first, so a response before the dilation cannot have followed from it. Both events need a definition. A dilation is a peak in the baseline-corrected diameter standing at least $0.05$\,mm above its surroundings, which is below the $0.1$ to $0.5$\,mm a task-evoked response spans, so the small ones are counted too. A response is taken to begin at the lowest point of the phasic component in the six seconds before its peak, since the detector marks peaks and the claim here is about onsets.

Each column is computed over a window, and the length of that window is swept rather than fixed, because estimates of this kind depend more on the window length than on the lag bound (Section~\ref{sec:combining-sensors-lit}). Three lengths are tried: five seconds, about one coupled episode; ten seconds, about two; and fifteen seconds, a deliberately long third case. At 4\,Hz these hold twenty, forty and sixty paired samples, which is little for a correlation on its own. All three are scored the same way and the best is carried forward.

A column can take a large value even when its two signals are unrelated, and the lag-searched column most of all, because taking the largest correlation across many shifts gives a high number whether or not the signals are coupled. The block is therefore computed a second time on a surrogate, with one signal of each pair rotated in time by a random offset, a scheme its authors call data sliding \citep{Moulder2018}. Rotating leaves each signal's own rhythm and distribution intact and breaks only the timing between the two, and it is repeated so the surrogate gives a range rather than a single value. The test is a narrow one. A column that beats the surrogate depends on the timing between its two signals. A column that does not beat it settles nothing, because the test cannot show that a pair is uncoupled.

The block is also scored on its own, as an Experiment-1-style row, so its contribution is visible before it is combined with anything else. The relationship is measured here, not learned; learning it is what the \ac{DCCA} arm does (Section~\ref{sec:methodology-alignment-alt}). Keeping the two apart is what lets each be judged separately.

Four combination mechanisms are run, each on every subset of the five sensors, so the result can be read across the mechanisms or down the subset sizes. The decision this experiment carries is nonetheless made on the full five-sensor set alone: the question is whether combining recovers more than the best single sensor, and selecting a subset would answer a different one while multiplying the comparisons. Every one of them also uses the standard model that Experiment~1 selects, so that a difference between two mechanisms is a difference between combination rules rather than between model families. The one arm that carries the cross-sensor block also uses the window selected for it in Section~\ref{sec:methodology-crossmodal-alt}. Each mechanism is either fitting-free or a single fit of that model, which keeps every arm on the same protocol as Experiment~1 and leaves none of them needing a nested refit.
\textbf{Early fusion} concatenates all five sensors' features into one matrix and trains the standard model on it, so that the model itself decides how to weigh the modalities against one another.

\textbf{Early fusion with the cross-sensor block} adds the eight engineered columns of Section~\ref{sec:methodology-crossmodal-alt} to that same matrix. Because the model and the sensor set are both unchanged, the difference between this arm and the previous one isolates the contribution of the cross-sensor block.

\textbf{Late fusion} leaves each sensor's own Experiment~1 pipeline intact and combines only the predictions that come out of it, one base model per modality \citep{Poria2017}. Two variants differ only in how those predictions are weighted. Simple averaging weights every sensor equally, whereas \ac{CCC}-weighted averaging weights each sensor by its own Experiment~1 \ac{CCC} for that slice, normalised so that the weights sum to one; weighting a decision-level average by how reliable each sensor has proved is established for wearable affect recognition \citep{Singh2026}. A sensor whose \ac{CCC} is negative is floored to zero weight before the weights are normalised, since a negative weight would invert that sensor's prediction rather than discount it.
Whichever of the four reaches the highest mean \ac{CCC} over the four slices is carried into Experiments~3 to~5, ties resolved as in Section~\ref{sec:protocol}.

From this experiment onward the target is ordinal rather than continuous: each rating is expressed as one of a small number of ordered levels, for the person-relative reasons given in Section~\ref{sec:protocol}. Discretising a continuous affect rating before prediction is established practice \citep{Jammot2025}, though usually as a two-class split rather than as ordered levels.

Experiments~1 and~2 fitted continuous regressors and scored them by \ac{CCC}. There are two ways to put an ordinal target on that starting point, and this experiment runs both rather than assuming one.

\textbf{The two arms.} The \textbf{trained-on-levels} arm fits a classifier against the binned rating directly, so the quantity it optimises is the quantity it is evaluated on. Its inputs are the feature matrix Experiment~2 carries forward: all five sensors' features concatenated, together with the cross-sensor block at the window that experiment selected. The \textbf{post-hoc} arm refits nothing: it takes the stored continuous predictions of that same matrix, produced by the mechanism Experiment~2 carries forward, and assigns them to levels after the fact, on the identical rows, so the only thing that changes between level counts is where the edges fall. Both arms therefore read the same features on the same rows and differ only in how the target is treated.

The trained-on-levels arm predicts a class, and its family treats the levels as unordered categories even though \ac{QWK} scores them by the square of the distance between the true level and the predicted one. The post-hoc arm keeps the order by construction, since it bins a continuous prediction. The comparison is therefore between a model scored on an ordinal metric it does not optimise and a predictor that preserves the ordering without being fitted to it. A model built for ordinal targets, which optimises the ordering directly, is not fitted here and remains a gap this comparison cannot close.

Both arms are swept at every candidate level count, and the arm carried forward is chosen from that sweep. Two things then follow from one decision: the level count is selected on the chosen arm's scores, and every binned result from Experiment~4 onward is read from the same arm, so the count a later experiment uses was chosen for the predictor that experiment runs.
The classifier's inputs are the sensor features alone. Valence and arousal are the source of the label and are never inputs, at training or at test.

Valence and arousal are discretised on their own axes, independently of one another, into equal-width levels on the known $0$--$10$ scale. The edges are fixed by design at equal spacing across that scale and are never fitted to the data.

\textbf{Odd against even level counts.} A joystick rating can settle at rest for extended stretches, so the parity of the level count matters where the instrument has a resting position. An odd count places the scale's midpoint inside a level; an even count places it exactly on a boundary between two. The two annotation streams differ here: rcea was moved continuously during the visit and has a resting position at the scale midpoint, while retro was drawn afterwards from a replay and has none. The share of readings sitting on that midpoint in each stream is reported in Section~\ref{sec:results-characterization-alt}. The parity preference therefore bears on the rcea slices and not on the retro ones. Both parities run the length of the sweep below, so the comparison holds across it rather than at one end. For each count, the share of readings landing exactly on the midpoint is recorded alongside whether that midpoint falls on an edge.

At each level count the trained-on-levels arm is fitted on the training participants' early-fusion features against their binned ratings, and predicts the held-out visitor's level from that visitor's features alone. Its family is the classifier counterpart of the family Experiment~1 selected, so it differs from the continuous arm in what it predicts rather than in which family predicts it. That classifier is extremely randomised trees, 300 trees of unrestricted depth, refitted in every fold with fixed hyperparameters and no per-fold tuning. Every difference this experiment compares falls far inside the pooled-\ac{QWK} selection resolution of $0.21$, so tuning could not change which arm or level count is carried. The evaluation protocol is that of Section~\ref{sec:protocol}, unchanged. The post-hoc arm is not fitted at any count: the stored prediction and the stored rating are assigned to levels by the same fixed edges and scored, so it costs no refitting and its folds are those of the prediction it inherits.

Both ordinal metrics, \ac{QWK} and balanced accuracy as defined in Section~\ref{sec:protocol}, are computed at every count. Balanced accuracy needs one further step before it can be compared across a sweep: its chance value is $1/B$, so it falls as the levels multiply whatever the model does. It is therefore compared against that chance value at each count, never against its own value at another count.

The sweep covers every count from 3 to 20. No consensus granularity is available to inherit (Section~\ref{sec:ordinal-lit}), and sweeping the whole range rather than a chosen handful leaves no question of why one set of candidates was preferred. It also shows what finer levels cost rather than asserting it, and it gives every count a neighbour of each parity, so a count is read against the ones either side of it and not on its own.

Scoring a count and selecting it are separate things. A level that few visitors ever occupy can be neither learned from the training participants nor scored on a held-out one, so a count is selectable only where every level holds at least one per cent of the rated seconds in both streams. That rule is fixed before any score is seen, and which counts it admits on this cohort is reported in Section~\ref{sec:results-exp3-range}. Counts above the cut are scored and reported at every stage, as the curve the selectable range is read against, and none of them is carried forward. Narrowing the field in advance also limits a second risk the configuration search already faces, that the best of many candidates reflects chance rather than a real difference \citep{Cawley2010}.

The selection resolution this sweep is read against is wide relative to the pooled \ac{QWK} an ordinal target is expected to reach at this cohort size, so the counts are expected to tie and the selection to fall to the tie-break rules of this section rather than to a difference between counts. The sweep's purpose is accordingly to establish whether any granularity lifts agreement above chance, not to identify the granularity that lifts it most.

The arm is decided first, and once for the whole experiment rather than per slice, because the arm chosen here is the one every binned figure from Experiment~4 onward reads and mixing arms between slices would make those figures incommensurable. Each arm is summarised by the mean of its pooled \ac{QWK} over the selectable counts and the four slices, and the comparison is resolved at the pooled \ac{QWK} selection resolution of Section~\ref{sec:protocol}: where the two fall inside that margin they are not separable at this cohort size and the trained-on-levels arm is kept, being the one that optimises the quantity it is scored on rather than inheriting a prediction fitted to a continuous loss. Both arms' full sweeps are reported whichever is carried forward.

The count carried into every later experiment is then decided on the selected arm, independently for each of the four condition-by-axis slices, with no requirement that the two streams or the two axes agree. Within a slice the decision is made on pooled \ac{QWK} alone, the one metric whose chance correction is commensurable across counts; balanced accuracy is reported at every count and checks the selected count against its own chance value rather than selecting it.

The choice is resolved at the same margin: counts whose pooled \ac{QWK} differs by less than it are treated as tied. Among tied counts the coarser is kept, as the more conservative candidate; where tied counts also differ in parity, the one placing the scale midpoint inside a level is preferred, since a rating that settles at rest sits exactly on that midpoint.

The selected count's stability is checked by a leave-one-participant-out jackknife. The comparison among the candidate counts is repeated with each participant held out in turn, and the fraction of repeats still selecting the same winner is reported alongside it. The repeats are recomputed from each count's stored per-participant scores.

Two linked questions are answered here. The first is whether affect is recovered more accurately when prediction is scoped to the painting a visitor is attending, rather than read from the whole session as a single stream. The second is how much affective signal was ever shared across visitors, and which sensors carry it. The two belong together, because whatever signal the visitors never shared sets a ceiling on what scoping to a painting could recover.

Each analysed second is labelled with the painting the visitor was attending, using the \ac{VR} engine's own gaze records. The engine casts a ray along the visitor's line of sight and registers whichever object it strikes. Each record that results names the painting struck, the sub-region within it, the moment the look began, how long it lasted, and how far the visitor stood from the object. The engine's timestamps are converted onto the sensor timeline, and a one-second row takes a painting's label when it falls inside a kept viewing episode of that painting. A second falling inside no episode receives no label, and is excluded from the localised evaluation.

The ray draws no distinction between a painting the visitor walked up to and one that crossed their line of sight from across the room. Two further conditions are therefore placed on a record before it can label a second, and a record failing either contributes no label at all rather than a weaker one.

The first condition is proximity. A record is kept only where the visitor stood closer to the painting than the ninety-fifth percentile of that visitor's own viewing distances across the five paintings. The bound is therefore taken from the data rather than set at a chosen number of metres, and it adapts to how close each visitor habitually stood. Where the bounds fall on this cohort is reported in Section~\ref{sec:results-localisation-alt}.

The second condition is dwell time. A single record is far shorter than one second, so the condition applies to viewing episodes rather than to records: consecutive records naming the same painting are merged into one episode, and an episode lasting less than a second is discarded. One second is the resolution of the labelled data, so a shorter episode could not fill an analysed second in any case.

Both conditions are fixed in advance and applied identically to every visitor and every painting. The same records also resolve smaller regions inside a painting, namely the artwork without its text panel and, for B3, three named objects (Figure~\ref{fig:vr-layout-alt}). Those finer regions are not used here, since this experiment works at the whole-painting level throughout.

Two models are compared. The first is the one already fitted on whole sessions in Experiments~2 and~3. The second is fitted here, on the attended rows alone, under the same leave-one-participant-out protocol. Each held-out visitor is then scored under both models, and in both cases the rows scored are that visitor's attended rows. The two models yield three quantities rather than two, because the rows a model trains on and the rows it is scored on have to be varied one at a time.

The \textbf{whole-session} quantity is the first model's result on the held-out visitor's entire session, and it is reported for context. Its continuous score is Experiment~2's early fusion of all five sensors together with the cross-sensor block (Section~\ref{sec:methodology-fusion-alt}), and its ordinal scores come from Experiment~3's trained-on-levels arm fitted on that same matrix (Section~\ref{sec:methodology-binning-alt}). The \textbf{whole-on-attended} quantity takes that model's held-out predictions unchanged and scores them on the visitor's attended rows alone, so that only the scored rows change. The \textbf{attended-trained} quantity is the second model, whose features, model family and fold structure are held exactly as for the whole session, so that only the rows it learns from differ.

Whole-on-attended against attended-trained is the comparison that answers the scoping question. Both are scored on identical rows of the same visitor, so the only thing separating them is whether the model learned from whole sessions or from attended rows. Comparing attended-trained against whole-session instead would change the training rows and the scored rows at once, and a difference could not then be attributed to either. Whole-session against whole-on-attended isolates the other change on its own, the effect of restricting the rows a model is judged on.

All three quantities are scored on the same three metrics. The continuous score comes from the regressor carried out of Experiment~2, and the two ordinal scores from Experiment~3's trained-on-levels classifier, fitted at the slice's selected level count and trained and scored on the same rows as the regressor for that quantity.

The comparison above pools all five paintings into a single set of attended rows. It is then repeated for each painting on its own. The attended rows are first split by the painting they belong to. Within one painting, the attended-trained model is refitted on the training participants' rows for that painting, and the whole-session model's held-out predictions are scored on the held-out visitor's rows for that painting. Folds, features and metrics are unchanged, so the only difference from the pooled comparison is the narrower set of rows. A painting that behaves unlike the rest is then visible in its own scores, rather than averaged into the pooled result.

A painting covers far fewer seconds than a whole visit. Every painting-scoped evaluation therefore rests on fewer rows than the whole-session one, and narrowing to a single painting reduces them again. The row and participant counts behind each quantity are reported alongside its scores (Section~\ref{sec:results-localisation-scoping-alt}). The whole-session model is not subsampled down to match, so the gap in row counts is a caveat the painting-scoped scores are read against rather than a variable this experiment controls.

Chance correction in \ac{QWK} is computed from the distribution of levels across the rows being scored, so changing the row set moves the correction as well as the prediction. Part of any movement in an ordinal score between two row sets is therefore a change in those level proportions, rather than a sign that any second was predicted better or worse. The headline comparison is made between two quantities scored on identical rows for exactly this reason, and the continuous score, which does not share the property, is reported beside the ordinal ones.

Any cell, whether pooled across paintings or narrowed to one, is reported only where it covers at least five participants and at least fifty rows. A cell failing either threshold is recorded as not reportable rather than omitted.

The differences this experiment looks for are expected to be small beside the spread between one visitor and the next, and the comparisons are numerous: one for each pair of quantities, on each painting and on the pooled set, in every slice. A difference of the size expected here would appear somewhere among them even if scoping changed nothing at all. Two safeguards follow from that. A paired test over per-participant scores asks whether a difference holds within visitors rather than across them, and controlling the false-discovery rate accounts for how many comparisons were made before any one of them is called real.

The scoping comparison is tested under the protocol of Section~\ref{sec:protocol}, with the correction spanning the five paintings, the two annotation streams and the two axes. The test runs twice on the same participants, once on per-participant \ac{CCC} and once on per-participant \ac{QWK}. The correction is applied inside each metric's own family rather than across the two taken together, so that neither result is diluted by the other, and a change is credited only where both metrics agree. Balanced accuracy is not tested, because it is available here only as a pooled figure. It is read for direction, and against its own chance value, beside the two tested metrics.

The tested comparison is whole-on-attended against attended-trained, paired within participant, since that is the pair scored on identical rows. Whole-session against whole-on-attended is tested the same way wherever the effect of restricting the scored rows is being claimed, so a reported gain or loss is always attributed to the change that produced it.

Every attended second carries three things: the rating given at that second, the visitor who produced it, and the painting that visitor was attending. The question asked here is how much of the spread in those ratings belongs to the visitor, how much to the painting, and how much to neither.

Answering it means estimating a single typical rating for the cohort as a whole, plus one offset for each visitor and one offset for each painting. A visitor's offset applies to every second of theirs, whatever painting they were facing at the time. A painting's offset applies to every visitor who faced it. Once both offsets have been subtracted, the remainder is the residual, the second-to-second movement that neither the visitor's identity nor the painting's explains.

The two offsets are crossed rather than nested, because every visitor could view every painting and no painting belongs to one visitor. The model therefore lets the two vary independently, and it does not require that every visitor viewed every painting; the coverage actually observed is reported in Section~\ref{sec:results-characterization-alt}.

Dividing each variance component by the sum of the three gives that source's share, and the three shares account for the whole rating between them. The painting share is the most that knowing which painting a visitor faced could ever contribute to predicting their rating, so it sets a ceiling on what scoping a model to the attended painting can add. The other two shares say where the rest of the rating sits: in stable differences between one visitor and another, and in movement within a visit that neither identity explains.

Taking the paintings as the targets and the visitors as the raters, the painting share is an intraclass correlation: the share of a rating attributable to which painting was viewed rather than to who was viewing it. A small painting share says that painting identity shifts the average rating little beside the differences between people and the movement within a visit.

With only five paintings, the painting share rests on the fewest independent units of the three, so it is not read from a single number. Four checks are therefore placed around it. A participant-level bootstrap gives it a confidence interval. A leave-one-painting-out refit shows whether any single painting drives it. An eta-squared variance ratio on the same rows estimates the same quantity by an entirely different route. Finally the split is refitted on one mean rating per visitor per painting, which reduces each visitor to a single value per painting and returns the painting share in the one-observation-per-cell form the intraclass correlation is normally reported in; the second-level split has a residual that also absorbs the movement within a painting, so the two are not expected to agree in size.

The same three-way split is then run on each sensor's own features, using this chapter's feature set, and rolled up to the five sensor categories. Each feature is decomposed by the crossed model, and a category's share is the mean over its features. Running the sensors and the ratings through one procedure puts their painting shares on the same footing, so that the two can be compared directly: a sensor whose painting share exceeds the ratings' tracks the painting more closely than the visitor's own reported feeling does. The one-way variance ratio is computed on the same rows, as the cross-check it also provides for the ratings, and is reported in the appendix.

One guard applies to the per-feature fits. A fit that drives its person or painting component to zero has not divided the variance at all: the surviving component absorbs what the collapsed one should have held, and the resulting share describes that collapse rather than the feature. Any fit placing a component below $0.05\%$ is therefore recorded as degenerate and left out of its category's mean, and the number excluded is reported beside the share.

The split is repeated once more on the binned target. Every ordinal result from this experiment onward is scored on levels rather than on the continuous rating, so the same crossed model is fitted to the level index at each slice's selected level count (Section~\ref{sec:methodology-binning-alt}). Reported beside the continuous split on the same rows, it shows whether discretising the target moves the shares that bound what any model could recover.
This decomposition is fitted on the ratings and the attended-row definition, neither of which depends on which model Experiment~2 selects, so it is not re-run once that model is chosen.

This experiment asks whether personalising the visitor-general model to each visitor recovers person-specific structure that model cannot use. Three levers are tested, each acting on the whole-session pipeline of Experiment~2 rather than the painting-localised variant of Experiment~4, and each evaluated under the protocol of Section~\ref{sec:protocol}.

The three differ in what they adapt: the features the model reads, the data it is trained on, and the target it predicts. Only the first asks nothing of the visitor beyond their unlabelled signals, and the other two require some of that visitor's own ratings. The reference each lever is judged against sees nothing the held-out visitor produced, so a difference between the two reflects the lever and nothing else that changed in the run.

\textbf{Scoring.} Every lever is scored on the same three metrics as Experiment~4, and from the same two models, with the lever applied identically to both. The continuous score is reported beside the ordinal ones for the reason given in Section~\ref{sec:protocol}: a chance-corrected agreement statistic moves whenever the level marginals move, and personalisation moves them directly. The person-relative target is the one exception. It redefines the level boundaries and leaves the regressor untouched, so its continuous score equals its reference's by construction, and it is reported rather than tested.

\textbf{The scored rows.} Each lever sets aside part of the visitor's session before anything is scored: the baseline lever takes the seconds before the first painting view, the warm-up takes the opening seconds it folds into training, and the person-relative target reads a held-out visitor's boundaries from that same opening stretch. All three levers and all their references are therefore scored on one common set of rows per visitor, those left once both the baseline window and the longest warm-up have been set aside. Figures from different levers can then be compared with one another, not only each with its own reference. Each reference is a no-personalisation counterpart computed fresh in the same run, under identical folds and on identical rows, never a figure carried over from an earlier experiment.

\textbf{Significance testing.} Each lever is tested against its reference by the paired test of Section~\ref{sec:protocol} on per-participant \ac{QWK}, with false-discovery correction applied within that lever's own family of tests. The same test is run on per-participant \ac{CCC} for the two levers whose continuous predictions differ from the reference's. The number of visitors whose score a lever improves is reported beside each gain, so a figure carried by a few visitors is visible as such rather than read as a cohort-wide effect.

Each visitor's own resting level is estimated from their unlabelled signals and removed before any model reads their features. Physiological levels differ between people for reasons unrelated to affect, so subtracting a person's own resting value is a simple way to make two visitors' features comparable (Section~\ref{sec:personalisation-lit}).

The window is the opening stretch of the visitor's session, running from the start of their analysed stream to the second before they first attended a painting. That boundary is already defined by Experiment~4's attention labelling and is not chosen again here. Within the window, each feature's median is taken for that visitor and subtracted from every row of that visitor's session. The median is used rather than the mean, so that a single artefact in a short window cannot move the offset.

The transform is fitted per person, from features alone. It uses no rating from anyone and no data from any other visitor, and it is applied to training and held-out visitors alike, which is what keeps it usable on a visitor the system has never met. A feature with no valid value inside a visitor's window keeps its raw values, since no offset can be estimated for it. The window is short and the cardiac features are aggregated over sixty seconds, so those are the features an offset is least likely to be available for.

A short labelled slice of the held-out visitor's own visit is folded into the population model's training, so the model is fitted on the other visitors together with a little of the one it will be scored on. It is the only lever that puts the visitor's own ratings into the model's training data, and it shows what those labels are worth when the model can learn from them directly.

The slice is the opening stretch of the visitor's annotated stream, since a deployment could collect it only at the start of a visit. Those rows are appended to the training set alongside every other visitor's, unweighted, and the model is refitted once per duration and per fold. The warm-up rows are never scored.

The duration is swept across 30, 60, 120, and 180 seconds, so the trade between annotation demanded and accuracy gained is read as a curve rather than at a single point. All four durations are scored on the same rows, those remaining after the longest of them, so the four points differ in how much labelled data entered training and in nothing else.

This lever adapts the target rather than the model, and it tests the person-relative argument that motivated discretisation (Section~\ref{sec:protocol}). Each level boundary is recomputed from a visitor's own ratings instead of sitting at the same absolute position for everyone.

The boundaries are placed at equal-frequency positions in that visitor's ratings, so that each level holds a comparable share of that visitor's seconds. Quantiles are used rather than an equal-width split of the visitor's own range, because a single extreme rating would otherwise fix the outer boundaries for the whole session. A training visitor's boundaries are computed from their full session. A held-out visitor's are computed from the opening slice alone, the same stretch the longest warm-up consumes, so this lever asks no more of the visitor than that one does.

The classifier is then fitted and scored on the redefined levels, and the fixed cohort-wide scheme is re-scored on identical rows, so the two definitions are compared on equal terms rather than across different row sets. The regressor is left untouched.

Before any model is fitted, three things about the analysed data bear on how every later result is read: how much of each sensor was actually recorded, how usable what was recorded is, and how the visitors moved through the exhibition.

The analysed data comprise 12,654 one-second observations from 22 participants in rcea and 6,880 from 16 participants in retro, 19,534 in total, after rows without an aligned annotation are removed. The feature matrices the experiments run on are assembled at a later stage and hold $12,660$ rcea and $7,022$ retro labelled seconds, six and 142 more; every percentage from Experiment~2 onward is taken against those counts. The two annotation streams differ in one respect that the later binning depends on. In rcea, $20.0\%$ of rated seconds on valence and $20.5\%$ on arousal sit exactly on the scale midpoint, the position at which an untouched joystick rests. In retro no rated second sits exactly there on either axis, since that stream was drawn retrospectively and has no resting position. Where a level boundary falls relative to the midpoint therefore matters for rcea and not for retro (Section~\ref{sec:methodology-binning-alt}).

\textbf{Eye tracker.} The logger writes one sample per rendered frame, so the tracker slows down whenever the headset renders a demanding scene, delivering a median $23$\,Hz over a session against the nominal $120$. Pauses longer than $100$\,ms add up to a median $57\%$ of a session, yet almost every second still contains samples, because the pauses are short and scattered (Table~\ref{tab:alt-coverage-summary}). The slowdown is worst at the paintings themselves: $18$ samples per second there against $47$ elsewhere, for 44 of the 45 participants with a usable viewing log. The two eyes' diameters agree at a median $r=0.92$; one participant (M38, $r=0.12$) is the exception and is kept.

\textbf{Teleports.} Walking and teleporting are easy to tell apart in the engine's position records. Walking moves a visitor at less than $2$\,m/s between one record and the next ($99.8\%$ of the 98,675 record pairs), while a teleport implies $4$ to $67$\,m/s; only 24 pairs fall between the two. At the $3$\,m/s threshold the cohort contains 172 teleports during viewing and 130 gaps between viewings that must contain one.

\textbf{Blood-volume pulse.} The wristband writes a sample exactly $64$ times per second in every recording, so this channel loses no samples and any fault in it lies in the values rather than in their spacing. Three visitors (M18, M26, M37) have no recording on it inside the session window.

\textbf{Electrodermal.} Twenty of the 47 recordings carry no usable signal. Eighteen are negative for at least half their length, and a skin conductance cannot be negative. Two more stay almost perfectly flat across the entire visit, varying by less than a single response would produce. These failures cluster in time rather than across visitors: 15 of the 22 recordings in the second collection wave are unusable, against 5 of the 25 in the first, which points to the electrodes wearing or losing contact as the study went on. On the 25 passing recordings that also carry temperature, the slow conductance level rises and falls with skin temperature over the visit (median Spearman $r=0.89$), while their second-to-second changes are unrelated (median $0.00$). The slow level therefore partly measures skin temperature and electrode contact, while the fast responses do not.

\textbf{Speech.} Visitors spoke little: speech is present in a median $6.9\%$ of a visitor's analysed seconds ($1.2$ to $23.0\%$, excluding the degenerate recording below). Eight transcripts are near-empty; one (M19) is a single word repeated by the recogniser over near-silence.

This experiment measures how much of a visitor's valence and arousal each sensor recovers on its own, for a visitor the model has never seen, and fixes the configuration and the model that every later experiment uses.

No sensor rises far above the chance-corrected floor on any axis or either annotation stream, and neither the searched configuration nor the model family changes that. Nothing this experiment varied moves the outcome, so whatever accounts for it lies outside the searched space. The explanation the rest of this thesis pursues is that what separates one visitor from another is larger than what moves within a single visit.

Every score reported here is a leave-one-subject-out \ac{CCC}. The selection resolution, below which two scores cannot be told apart, was measured before anything was compared, by the procedure of Section~\ref{sec:protocol}. The twenty repeats return answers from $-0.031$ to $+0.074$, four of them negative and sixteen positive on identical inputs, and their fifth and ninety-fifth percentiles differ by $0.078$. Rounded up, that is the selection resolution of $0.08$: two scores closer to one another than that are treated as indistinguishable throughout this thesis. On pooled \ac{QWK} the same twenty repeats give a gap of $0.204$, rounded up to the selection resolution of $0.21$ used from Experiment~3 onward.

Five parameters were searched, and none of them altered the outcome. The largest difference any parameter produced was $0.036$ mean \ac{CCC}, between trailing and forward cardiac windows on retro, and no other parameter moved it by more than $0.016$. In every sweep the variation between visitors was at least twice the variation between candidates. Each parameter was therefore decided by the tie rule rather than by its score, and every candidate with its spread is reported in Appendix~\ref{app:alt-experiment1}.

The configuration carried forward is the 30 degrees per second fixation rule, the uncorrected diameter, trailing windows at zero delay for pupil and \ac{HRV}, an interbeat multiplier of three, and the NeuroKit decomposition under the five-deviation mask with a three-second window. With the lengths fixed in Section~\ref{sec:methodology-unimodal}, each sensor is therefore aggregated over eight seconds for pupil, three for \ac{EDA}, sixty for \ac{HRV}, and one utterance for either speech channel. The sweep establishes that these settings cannot be told apart, not that the selected ones are preferable. It also removes one explanation for the near-zero scores, since no candidate of these five parameters moved the score.

No feature relates to the ratings consistently, before any model is fitted at all. Each feature is correlated with each rating axis within each visitor rather than across the cohort, so that differences between people cannot appear as a relation. Of the 436 tests, none survives correction for the number of tests performed, and the lowest adjusted $q$ value is $0.67$. Fourteen tests reach significance before that correction is applied. The coefficients are larger on retro than on rcea, but they rest on fewer visitors per test, so the difference reflects cohort size rather than a stronger relation (Table~\ref{tab:alt-exp1-relations-by-sensor}).

The strongest apparent relation belongs to the apparatus rather than to the visitor. The headset renders more slowly when a visitor stops at a painting (Section~\ref{sec:results-characterization-alt}), so a window covering an attended painting contains fewer samples than one covering a corridor. A saccade cannot be detected in samples that were never recorded. Saccade frequency therefore tracks the number of samples in the window. That is a correlation between two features rather than with a rating, and it is strong: a median within-visitor $0.92$ on retro and $0.90$ on rcea, never below $0.80$ for any visitor. Its correlation with retro arousal, $-0.37$, is the largest of the 436; the literature does not agree on the direction that relation should take, so it enters no directional comparison below.

Where the literature commits to a direction, the observed signs agree no more often than chance. Of the 114 features tested, 16 carry a direction stated in the modality literature reviewed in Chapter~\ref{chap:related-work}, compiled with their sources in Table~\ref{tab:alt-app-exp1-literature}, giving 28 directional cells across the two streams. Twelve agree with the predicted sign and sixteen run against it, a rate a binomial test cannot separate from chance ($p=0.57$), and no cell survives correction (Table~\ref{tab:alt-app-exp1-literature}). Confidence in the source does not help: the sixteen cells whose source is rated high-confidence agree in five, against five of ten at medium confidence. The disagreement is not confined to one sensor either: the speech acoustic features agree in six cells of ten, the cardiac features in three of eight, pupil in two of four, speech content in one of two, and the electrodermal features in none of four.

The disagreements are consistent across the two streams rather than scattered. Of the twelve features testable on both streams, four agree on both, four run opposite on both, and four disagree between streams. Pupil diameter is the clearest prediction that holds, rising with arousal on both streams and reaching $+0.31$ on retro, the largest coefficient of the 28; harmonics-to-noise ratio, jitter and shimmer also hold. Mean interbeat interval, fixation duration, pitch and loudness run against their predicted sign on both streams, loudness and mean interbeat interval despite high-confidence predictions. The cardiac features split: three of them match the predicted negative relation to arousal on retro and reverse on rcea.

Individual features therefore carry little of the rating, as the dataset's origin also found (Section~\ref{sec:bas-findings}), and every coefficient is mapped in Appendix~\ref{app:alt-experiment1} (Figure~\ref{fig:exp1-relations-heatmap}). Features this weak may still combine, and the remainder of this experiment measures whether they do.

No model family separates from the others. Across their twenty cell means the eight span $0.0124$ \ac{CCC}, a sixth of the selection resolution, and the summaries of Table~\ref{tab:alt-experiment1-families} rank them in orders that contradict one another. The highest mean belongs to CatBoost, which wins four cells against support-vector regression's five; the narrowest spread belongs to ridge, a reference rather than a candidate; and the single highest cell of the experiment, $+0.119$, belongs to the random forest, whose mean is the lowest of the eight.

Among the tree ensembles, which are the only candidates (Section~\ref{sec:methodology-unimodal}), CatBoost leads extremely randomised trees by $0.0007$, a hundredth of the selection resolution, so the two are tied and the tie resolves toward the family whose cells vary least, $0.034$ against $0.043$. Extremely randomised trees are carried, and that choice is arbitrary on this cohort rather than an advantage established over the alternatives.

\insightsbox{Findings}{%
\begin{itemize}
\item No sensor recovers the valence or arousal of an unseen visitor in this cohort. All twenty sensor-by-slice scores fall between $-0.072$ and $+0.084$, against a value of $0$ for a model carrying no information about that visitor.
\item Neither the settings searched nor the model families compared account for this. Five settings were searched and eight model families compared, and the families span $0.0124$, well inside the $0.08$ selection resolution.
\item The features do not relate to the ratings either. Of 436 tests of a feature against a rating, none survives correction.
\item Experiment~2 inherits these settings, extremely randomised trees, and a selection resolution of $0.08$, below which two scores are treated as indistinguishable.
\end{itemize}}

This experiment asks whether combining the sensors recovers more than any sensor recovers alone, and answers in three steps: how the timelines are reconciled, what a block of cross-sensor columns adds, and which combination mechanism to carry.

Combining sensors recovers no more than the best single sensor does. Neither of the two things fusion could have supplied, a better reconciliation of the timelines or a measurement of how two sensors move together, changes the outcome, and every difference among the mechanisms falls inside the selection resolution measured in Experiment~1. Every arm's per-participant scores, and every sensor subset under every mechanism, are given in Appendix~\ref{app:alt-experiment2}.

Four alignment methods were compared, and they cannot be told apart. Their means across the four slices span $0.006$, from $+0.0177$ for \ac{DTW} to $+0.0236$ for \ac{DCCA}, against a selection resolution of $0.08$ (Table~\ref{tab:alt-alignment-arms}). Within every cell the spread across visitors is between $0.045$ and $0.110$, eight to nineteen times the gap between the arms. The ordering is not stable either: the arm that scores lowest on rcea valence scores highest on rcea arousal.

Fixed windowing is carried forward. The four arms are tied within the selection resolution, and fixed windowing is the one arm that learns nothing from the data, which makes it the simplest of the tied candidates. Learned projections rank first by $0.004$, a twentieth of the selection resolution, so nothing here shows that projecting the pairs into a correlated space helps. The best single cell, retro valence under \ac{DCCA} at $+0.062$, remains below the $+0.084$ ceiling Experiment~1 left. The warped block is missing on an eighth of the retro rows, which thins \ac{DTW} and \ac{DCTW} in the two slices where they already score lowest.

The cross-sensor block does not score above its own surrogate. Of the twelve cells (three window lengths crossed with the four slices), one exceeds the ninety-fifth percentile of its surrogate distribution, and testing twelve cells at that percentile is expected to produce $0.6$ by chance alone. That one cell, rcea arousal at five seconds, exceeds its surrogate by $0.0003$. Six of the twelve fall below their surrogate's own mean, and four are negative (Table~\ref{tab:alt-crosssensor}).

The surrogate makes those figures readable, because it does not lie at zero. The block still scores between $+0.005$ and $+0.014$ on average once the timing between two signals is destroyed and everything else is left intact, and it scores higher the longer the window. The largest of the twelve cells, rcea valence at fifteen seconds, is $+0.0376$, which would read as the strongest result in Experiment~2 against a zero reference; its own surrogate reaches $+0.0390$ at the ninety-fifth percentile, so it falls below the null against which it was measured.

Five seconds is carried forward. The three windows span $0.0122$ in mean \ac{CCC}, well inside the selection resolution of $0.08$, so they are tied and the shortest is kept as the simpler candidate. The ordering is less arbitrary than the tie suggests when it is read against the surrogates rather than against zero: five seconds is the only length whose observed mean is not below its own surrogate mean, and the longer windows score higher under rotation than they do on the original timing. The block carries a value on 12,625 of the 12,660 rcea rows, so what it reports is not thinned by missing columns.

No combination of sensors scores above the best single sensor. Across all 31 subsets, three mechanisms and four slices, the highest score of any combination is $+0.0822$, reached by the pupil with the cardiac features under weighted averaging on retro valence; the highest score of any single sensor is $+0.0822$, reached by the cardiac features alone on the same slice. Both fall below the $+0.084$ that Experiment~1 left. Slice by slice, two combinations improve on the best single sensor, by $+0.016$ and $+0.021$, one falls short of it by $0.010$, and one matches it, and all four differences lie inside the selection resolution of $0.08$.

The direction in which the mean moves as sensors are added depends on the combination rule. Under early fusion and weighted averaging the mean rises with each sensor added, from $+0.0049$ to $+0.0199$ and from $+0.0073$ to $+0.0170$; under simple averaging it falls, from $+0.0049$ to $+0.0018$. Equal weights average the sensor that scores highest with four that score lower, whereas the other two rules can leave a sensor unused. Every one of those movements lies inside the selection resolution, so the direction can be stated but the difference cannot be established: no subset is selected from this table, and the group means are read as a description rather than as a search for the best combination.

Two patterns hold across the whole table. The mechanisms agree on which subsets score well: over the 26 subsets of more than one sensor, early fusion ranks them as weighted averaging does at $\rho=0.54$ and as simple averaging does at $\rho=0.52$, each averaged over the four slices, and early fusion shares no machinery with either beyond the sensors it is given. The two averaging rules agree more closely with one another, at $\rho=0.67$, which is what sharing one set of per-sensor fits would produce. The slices do not, however, agree on a sensor. The best single sensor is the cardiac features on rcea arousal, the electrodermal features on rcea valence, the pupil on retro arousal, and the cardiac features again on retro valence; the cardiac features are the best sensor of the five on one retro slice at $+0.082$ and the worst on the other at $-0.074$, on the same visitors. The ordering of subsets is reproducible, and the sensor that carries it is not.

The cross-sensor block was added to every subset, and it helps most where its own inputs are absent. Over all 31 subsets it raises the mean by $+0.0042$ and improves 25 of them. That improvement is concentrated on the 27 subsets that lack at least one of the pupil, electrodermal and cardiac sensors, where it gains $+0.0047$ and improves 23; on the four subsets that do contain all three it gains $+0.0010$ and improves two. The block is computed from those three signals whichever sensors a subset names, so on a subset that excludes them it supplies their information rather than the relationship between them. Where the three are present already, it adds almost nothing.

The selection resolution was measured on one cell of Experiment~1, with a different model family and a much narrower feature matrix, so whether it describes the spread of these arms was assumed rather than tested. Each of the four was therefore run five times over, differing only in the seed and in a resampling of each fold's training participants, the same procedure that produced the selection resolution in Experiment~1. Early fusion moves between repeats by $0.012$ to $0.062$ across the four slices, and early fusion with the block by $0.016$ to $0.062$, both inside the selection resolution of $0.08$. Weighted averaging moves by $0.078$ to $0.251$ and simple averaging by $0.036$ to $0.095$. The selection resolution therefore holds for the arm carried forward and fails for the averaging rules, which recompute their weights inside every fold and inherit the noise in those weights on top of the model's own. Five repeats put the fifth and ninety-fifth percentiles close to the extremes, so these are coarse estimates of a spread rather than precise ones, and they bear on how far the mechanisms can be told apart rather than on the score of any single arm.

Early fusion of all five sensors with the cross-sensor block is carried into Experiments~3 to~5. It records the highest mean of the four columns of Table~
ef{tab:alt-fusion-sizes}, the three mechanisms and early fusion with the block, $+0.0271$ against $+0.0199$, $+0.0170$ and $+0.0018$, and the highest mean is the criterion Section~\ref{sec:methodology-combination-alt} fixes. The four means fall inside the selection resolution, so the ordering among them is not established, and the block carries the qualification of Section~\ref{sec:results-crosssensor-alt}: scored on its own it does not rise above its rotated surrogate.

\insightsbox{Findings}{%
\begin{itemize}
\item Combining sensors recovers no more than the best single sensor. Both reach $+0.0822$ in their best cell.
\item Reconciling the sensors' timelines does not improve recovery. The four alignment methods span $0.006$, against the selection resolution of $0.08$.
\item Measuring how two sensors move relative to one another does not improve it either. Those columns exceed their own rotated surrogate in $1$ of $12$ cells, where chance alone produces $0.6$.
\item Experiment~3 inherits early fusion of all five sensors with the cross-sensor block, the highest of those four columns at $+0.0271$, and a second selection resolution of $0.21$ in the units of the ordinal score.
\end{itemize}}
This experiment asks whether a coarser, ordinal target recovers more of a visitor's rating than the continuous one did, and how many levels that target should have.
On this cohort, ordered levels do not lift agreement above chance at any granularity, and no count separates from any other.

Eighteen level counts are scored and five can be carried. Every level holds at least one per cent of the rated seconds in both streams up to seven, where the emptiest holds $1.72\%$. At eight it falls to $0.44\%$ and keeps falling, reaching $0.03\%$ at twenty. Counts above seven are therefore scored but never selectable.

The two arms cannot be told apart. Averaged over the five selectable counts the trained-on-levels arm reaches $-0.0387$ pooled \ac{QWK} and the post-hoc arm $-0.0510$, a difference of $0.0123$ against the selection resolution of $0.21$ (Table~\ref{tab:alt-exp3-arms}). Both peak at five levels, at $-0.0248$ and $-0.0431$. The trained-on-levels arm is carried forward under the tie rule of Section~\ref{sec:methodology-binning-alt}.

Positive agreement appears on one slice only. Of the 72 cells in each sweep, 17 are positive on the trained-on-levels arm and every one of them is retro valence; 19 are positive on the post-hoc arm, all retro valence but one. Restricted to the five selectable counts, that is five cells of twenty and six of twenty.

Balanced accuracy agrees (Table~\ref{tab:alt-exp3-ba}). It tracks its own chance value at every count, averaging, on the trained-on-levels arm, $0.312$ against a chance of $0.333$ at three levels and $0.137$ against $0.143$ at seven, and over the 144 cells of both sweeps it exceeds chance in 64, with a largest excess over chance of $0.041$. A model predicting one level for every second scores exactly $1/B$, and an excess of at most $0.041$ does not separate the sensors from such a model.

7 & $-0.0598$ & $-0.0732$ & $+0.0934$ & $-0.1166$ & $-0.0606$ & $-0.0292$ & $+0.0930$ & $-0.2172$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{adjustbox}
\end{table}

No count separates from any other in any slice. Within each slice the five selectable counts span at most $0.110$ pooled \ac{QWK} on the trained-on-levels arm and $0.147$ on the post-hoc arm, and across all eighteen counts the trained-on-levels mean over slices moves by $0.054$, so the whole sweep lies inside the selection resolution of $0.21$. Three levels is carried in every slice, as the coarsest of the tied counts. Being odd, it also places the scale midpoint inside a level rather than on a boundary. That preference bears on rcea, where one rated second in five sits exactly on the midpoint, and not on retro, where none does.

The ordering among the tied counts is nonetheless stable. Repeating the comparison with each visitor held out in turn, ranking the counts on the mean per-participant \ac{QWK}, returns the same best count in $91\%$, $100\%$, $75\%$ and $100\%$ of repeats across the four slices. Counts indistinguishable in size are ranked consistently, which is the pattern Experiment~2 reports for its sensor subsets.

The negative pooled scores are a property of pooling, not of the individual predictions. Pooled \ac{QWK} computes one chance correction from the marginals of every visitor's rows taken together, while the same predictions scored inside each visitor and then averaged give a different answer, and on three of the four slices a different sign. At five levels on the trained-on-levels arm, rcea arousal is $-0.0582$ pooled and $+0.0130$ per participant, rcea valence $-0.0486$ and $+0.0047$, retro arousal $-0.0597$ and $+0.0575$. Retro arousal reaches $-0.1585$ on the post-hoc arm at that count, and comes from visitors whose own median is $+0.0019$ and who are negative in seven cases of sixteen.

Mixing visitors whose level distributions differ makes a prediction that tracks each visitor around their own centre look systematically wrong once every visitor enters one confusion matrix. This is the same between-person confound the within-participant correlations of Section~\ref{sec:results-relations-alt} are computed to avoid. Pooled \ac{QWK} remains the headline, since Section~\ref{sec:protocol} fixes it in advance, and the per-participant figures stand beside it because the gap between them is a limitation of the metric rather than a result about the sensors.

\insightsbox{Findings}{%
\begin{itemize}
\item Discretising the rating into ordered levels does not raise agreement above chance. Pooled agreement is negative on every slice but retro valence, and balanced accuracy exceeds its chance value by at most $0.041$.
\item Granularity makes no difference. Across eighteen counts the trained-on-levels mean moves $0.054$, against the selection resolution of $0.21$.
\item Only five counts are selectable. Above seven levels some level holds under one per cent of the rated seconds, falling to $0.03\%$ at twenty.
\item Experiment~4 inherits three levels and the trained-on-levels arm.
\end{itemize}}

\section{Experiment 4: Localisation to the Attended Painting (RQ3, RQ4)}
\label{sec:results-localisation-alt}
blocks.body: This experiment asks whether scoping prediction to the attended painting recovers more affect than the whole session does, and how much of a rating the painting accounts for. Visitors stood close to the paintings they looked at: the 101,043 gaze records give a median viewing distance of $1.67$\,m, with the middle half between $1.34$ and $2.01$\,m and a tail reaching $17.7$\,m where the ray crossed a painting on the far side of the room. The proximity bound, each visitor's own ninety-fifth percentile, falls between $1.58$ and $6.31$\,m across the 46 visitors with a movement log, with a median of $2.47$\,m. Together the bounds keep $95,969$ of the $101,043$ records.

Dwell removes far more than proximity does. Merging consecutive records of the same painting gives 2,100 viewing episodes, of which 1,303 last a second or longer; the $38.0\%$ discarded are glances too short to fill an analysed second. The surviving episodes last a median of $4.2$\,s, and the longest lasts $223$\,s.

That leaves $7,986$ attended seconds on rcea, $63.1\%$ of that stream's analysed rows, and $4,134$ on retro, $58.9\%$. The five paintings carry between 1,274 and 1,947 of the rcea seconds each and between 549 and 1,110 of the retro ones, so no painting dominates the attended set. Three visitors contributed no attended second at all, M04 and M07 on rcea and M28 on retro, which leaves at most 20 of the 22 rcea visitors and 15 of the 16 retro ones in the localised evaluations below. Appendix~\ref{app:alt-experiment4} gives every quantity per held-out visitor, the paired tests in full, the per-painting grid, and every feature's own variance decomposition.

Scoping the prediction to the attended painting does not recover more affect. The headline comparison, whole-on-attended against attended-trained on identical rows, produces no credited difference in any slice on either tested metric: none of the 48 paired tests survives correction (Table~\ref{tab:alt-exp4-scoping}, with the tests in Table~\ref{tab:alt-app-exp4-tests}).

The comparison that answers the scoping question is the second row of each block against the third, which are scored on identical rows.}
\label{tab:alt-exp4-scoping}

The direction is against localisation rather than merely undecided. Training on the attended rows raises the continuous score in two of the four slices and lowers the ordinal score in all four, so the two metrics never agree on a gain and the rule requiring both to move together credits nothing. Averaged over the slices the movement is $+0.0026$ \ac{CCC}, $-0.0531$ pooled \ac{QWK} and $-0.0218$ balanced accuracy. On rcea the whole-session model scores $+0.0067$ and $+0.0165$ \ac{CCC} on valence and arousal, and the attended-trained model $-0.0113$ and $-0.0204$; on retro the same pairs are $+0.0646$ against $+0.0258$ and $+0.0207$ against $+0.0221$.

Restricting only the scored rows costs more than retraining on them. The second comparison, whole-session against whole-on-attended, has its own family of 48 tests. Here the continuous score falls in every slice, by $0.0435$ on rcea arousal and $0.0460$ on retro valence over the visitors entering the paired test. Two of the 48 tests survive correction on \ac{CCC} alone, and both are losses on painting B2: rcea arousal falls from $+0.0264$ to $-0.0686$ ($q=0.019$, three of twenty visitors improved) and retro valence from $+0.0398$ to $-0.0429$ ($q=0.035$, none of fourteen improved). Their \ac{QWK} counterparts do not survive ($q=0.55$ and $q=0.95$), so neither loss is credited under the rule that a difference must survive on both metrics. The direction can still be stated: narrowing the rows a model is scored on lowers the continuous score, while no comparison shows a gain from narrowing the rows it is trained on.

Narrowing to a single painting settles nothing either, and it does so on complete evidence: every one of the 60 cells clears both reporting thresholds, covering at least five participants and at least fifty rows, so none is recorded as not reportable.

The cells divide almost evenly. Attended-trained exceeds whole-on-attended in 10 of the 20 painting-by-slice cells on \ac{CCC}, 9 on pooled \ac{QWK} and 8 on balanced accuracy, which is what an absent effect looks like. Four cells improve on all three metrics at once, B1 on retro arousal, B2 on rcea arousal, B3 on rcea valence and B3 on retro valence, and none of the four survives correction. Two cells beat the whole-session figure outright, both on retro arousal: B1 at $+0.0717$ and C6 at $+0.0530$ against $+0.0207$. Both gaps fall inside the selection resolution of $0.08$, and neither was corrected for the size of the sweep, so both are leads rather than results.

There is almost nothing shared to recover. Fitted on the attended rows, the crossed model puts between $0.1\%$ and $1.5\%$ of a visitor's rating on the painting being viewed, against $36.4\%$ to $64.5\%$ on a stable difference between visitors and $35.4\%$ to $62.1\%$ on movement within the visit that neither explains (Table~\ref{tab:alt-exp4-variance}). The three shares sum to one hundred per cent in every slice.

The last two columns repeat the painting share on the binned target and on one mean rating per visitor per painting, at which point it is the intraclass correlation between visitors.}

The painting share is small under every check and imprecise under one of them. A one-way variance ratio on identical rows returns $0.80\%$ to $3.33\%$, the same order by an entirely different route. Refitting with each painting dropped in turn moves it between $0.8$ and $1.9$ on rcea valence and between $4.1$ and $9.8$ on retro arousal, where the point estimate is $0.1$; a single stimulus therefore carries a large part of what little there is. The participant-cluster bootstrap is wide, running from $0.1$ to $17.3$ at its worst, which is the five-painting limit showing directly: this cohort can establish that the painting share is small and cannot locate it precisely.

Discretising the target does not change the picture. At three levels the painting share reads $0.3\%$ to $3.7\%$ and the person share $32.0\%$ to $55.3\%$, so the ordinal results are read against the same bound as the continuous ones.

Averaging away the movement within a visit does not uncover a shared response either. Reduced to one mean rating per visitor per painting, 100 cells on rcea and 71 on retro, the painting share falls to $0.0\%$ on three slices and $0.2\%$ on the fourth, and the person share rises to between $64.3\%$ and $79.9\%$. Read as an intraclass correlation with paintings as targets and visitors as raters, that is an agreement of $0.000$ to $0.002$, which this cohort cannot separate from none at all.

Several sensors track the painting more closely than the ratings do. Rolled up to the categories, the painting share runs from $0.27\%$ for the cross-sensor block to $3.85\%$ for the electrodermal features. On rcea, where the ratings' own share is $1.5\%$ and $1.2\%$, the speech acoustic features at $2.98\%$ and the pupil at $1.87\%$ exceed it; on retro, where the ratings fall to $0.1\%$, every one of the six categories does, the electrodermal features by a factor of thirty-eight. That ordering is not evidence that those sensors are the more affect-informative. The cardiac features are the most person-locked of the set, at $66.2\%$ and $56.9\%$ across the two streams. The category means rest on very different numbers of features, 88 acoustic against one content feature, so they are not equally precise, and 35 of the 244 per-feature fits collapsed a component to the boundary and were excluded.

\insightsbox{Findings}{%
\begin{itemize}
\item Scoping prediction to the attended painting does not recover more affect. None of the 48 paired tests on identical rows survives correction.
\item Two losses on painting B2 survive correction on the continuous score alone: rcea arousal falls from $+0.0264$ to $-0.0686$ and retro valence from $+0.0398$ to $-0.0429$. Neither is credited, because \ac{QWK} does not confirm them.
\item Little shared signal exists to recover. The painting accounts for $0.1\%$ to $1.5\%$ of a rating and the visitor for $36.4\%$ to $64.5\%$, and two visitors viewing the same painting agree at $0.000$ to $0.002$.
\item Experiment~5 inherits the whole-session pipeline, since localisation established no gain to carry.
\end{itemize}}

This experiment asks whether adapting the model to the held-out visitor recovers the person-specific structure Experiment~4 located. The levers move the pooled figures in the direction personalisation would predict and never by enough to credit. Across the 24 lever-by-slice cells, pooled \ac{QWK} rises in 21, balanced accuracy in 20 and \ac{CCC} in 15 (Table~\ref{tab:alt-exp5-levers}, with each lever's movement against its reference in Table~\ref{tab:alt-app-exp5-deltas}). Every arm is scored on the same rows, the $8,700$ rcea and $3,980$ retro seconds left once the baseline window and the longest warm-up are set aside, so the arms are comparable to one another and not only to their own references. Appendix~\ref{app:alt-experiment5} gives every arm per held-out visitor on both metrics, together with the paired tests.

The labelled warm-up is the one lever with an ordered response. Its pooled \ac{QWK} rises with every extra second of the visitor's own annotation on three of the four slices. At 180 seconds it reaches $+0.2717$ on retro valence, $+0.1798$ on retro arousal and $+0.1035$ on rcea arousal, rises of $+0.1985$, $+0.3019$ and $+0.2268$ over the reference; on rcea valence it dips between 30 and 60 seconds before reaching $+0.0815$. Its continuous score stands above the reference on all four slices at that length, most on retro arousal, from $+0.0248$ to $+0.0902$.

Baseline-window calibration splits the two metrics. It lowers the continuous score on three of the four slices, by up to $0.0393$ on retro valence, while raising pooled \ac{QWK} on three and balanced accuracy on three. A lever that moves an ordinal score and a continuous one in opposite directions on the same rows is shifting the level marginals rather than predicting any second better.

The person-relative target is the clearest case of the same effect. Recomputing each visitor's level boundaries from their own ratings leaves the regressor untouched, so its continuous score equals the reference's exactly in all four slices, while pooled \ac{QWK} rises in every one, by $+0.0679$ to $+0.1682$. The entire movement is a change in what the levels mean, bought with an early slice of the held-out visitor's own annotation, and none of it is evidence that a second was predicted better.

No lever earns a credited gain. None of the 48 paired tests survives correction, on either metric and in any slice, and the smallest adjusted value anywhere is $q=0.138$ (Table~\ref{tab:alt-app-exp5-tests}). Four of the 48 compare quantities that are identical by construction, the person-relative target's continuous score against its reference, so 44 are informative.

The strongest single result falls well short. A 180-second warm-up on rcea arousal raises per-participant \ac{CCC} from $+0.0217$ to $+0.0739$ and improves 16 of the 22 visitors, at an uncorrected $p=0.0066$ that becomes $q=0.138$ once the family is accounted for. Two comparisons in the experiment would clear an uncorrected threshold: this one, and a 60-second warm-up on rcea valence at $p=0.0115$, which corrects to the same $q$.

Two readings survive these data. Either the levers do nothing, or they help some visitors by enough to move a pooled figure that a paired test over 12 to 22 visitors cannot resolve. The warm-up's response is ordered across three slices, which favours the second reading without separating it from noise at this cohort size. The result is a null at 12 to 22 visitors rather than evidence against personalisation.

The lever with the best evidence is also the one that asks the most of a visitor, since the warm-up uses the visitor's own moment-to-moment ratings. The person-relative target needs the same annotation, and its movement comes from the level definition rather than from the prediction. Baseline-window calibration is the only lever that needs no rating from the visitor, and it is the one on which the two metrics disagree.

\textbf{RQ1, how accurately each sensor and combination recovers affect.} No sensor separates from the chance-corrected floor: the twenty sensor-by-slice scores fall between $-0.072$ and $+0.084$ \ac{CCC}. No combination of sensors scores above the best single sensor: both reach $+0.0822$. The means of the five sensors, of the eight model families and of the four alignment methods each span less than the $0.08$ selection resolution, so within none of the three sets can one member be told apart from another.

\textbf{RQ2, whether an ordinal target recovers more.} On this cohort, ordered levels do not lift agreement above chance at the levels swept, and the two arms differ by $0.0123$ against the selection resolution of $0.21$, which leaves them indistinguishable.

\textbf{RQ3, whether scoping to the attended painting recovers more.} It does not. None of the 48 paired tests on identical rows survives correction. The only surviving differences are two losses on the continuous score from restricting the rows a model is scored on, and neither is credited because \ac{QWK} does not confirm them.

\textbf{RQ4, where the variance sits.} Far more of a rating is attributable to the person than to the painting: between $36.4\%$ and $64.5\%$ of a rating is attributable to who was viewing, against $0.1\%$ to $1.5\%$ attributable to which painting was viewed. The split is computed on the self-reports alone, so it holds for any pipeline applied to these data.

\textbf{RQ5, whether personalising recovers person-specific structure.} It is not established at this cohort size. The pooled figures rise in 21 of the 24 cells, but no paired test survives correction, and the smallest adjusted value is $q = 0.138$. The only lever whose gain grows with the annotation it is given is the labelled warm-up, which trains on the visitor's own ratings.

Most of the limitations on these conclusions sit in the paradigm, the cohort, and the annotation streams, and few in any processing choice, because the ceiling reported here is set by the labels themselves.

\textbf{Naturalistic, low-intensity setting.} The paradigm elicits affect too gently for the sensors to read it reliably. A free-roaming \ac{VR} museum is calm and self-paced, and its paintings are static and viewed at leisure, so the affect it elicits falls well short of the strong, well-separated states laboratory elicitation produces. Natural behaviour remains in the data: walking, stopping and returning to a painting modulate the cardiac and electrodermal signals independently of affect, and uncontrolled scene luminance leaves the pupil signal conflated with the light and content of the painting. Since the paradigm's purpose was a natural visit, none of these influences was controlled or modelled as a covariate.

\textbf{Cohort and stimuli.} Every estimate rests on 22 or 16 people and never on the 38 collected, because the two annotation streams are analysed separately throughout. Both streams are small and draw on disjoint groups of visitors, so every \ac{LOSO} estimate is noisy. The configuration search compared candidate sets fixed in advance, so it samples preprocessing choices at named, literature-grounded points rather than searching them exhaustively. Questions that require subgroups, such as whether clusters of similar responders exist, are out of reach at this size.

\textbf{Sensors and person-level information.} The correspondence between an autonomic correlate and a reported feeling is not fixed across people, which bounds what any pipeline applied to these features can recover. None of the five sensors observes valence or arousal: the labels are self-reports and the features are autonomic and attentional correlates. The aligned dataset carries no demographic, questionnaire, personality or affect-disposition measure.

This thesis asked whether a museum guide could recover a visitor's valence and arousal at one-second resolution from wearable sensors, for a visitor it has never seen. Visitors moved freely through a \ac{VR} museum of five paintings wearing an eye tracker, a wristband recording skin conductance and heart rate, and a microphone, and rated their own valence and arousal either continuously during the visit (rcea) or retrospectively over a replay (retro). Every model was trained on all visitors but one and scored on the one held out. Scores are chance-corrected: zero is what a model that knows nothing about the visitor would obtain, and a model is useful only if it rises clearly above that floor. None did so. Every claim below is about this collection and not about the paradigm in general. Section~\ref{sec:discussion-hard-alt} explains why. Sections~\ref{sec:discussion-localisation-alt} and~\ref{sec:discussion-shared-alt} examine the two design choices that might have moved the result. Section~\ref{sec:discussion-guide-alt} sets out the consequences for a guide.

The dominant cause is in the ratings. Each rating was split into a part that belongs to the visitor, a part that belongs to the painting, and a remainder. A model trained on other people can only use the painting part, because only that part recurs across people. It is $0.1\%$ to $1.5\%$ of a rating; the visitor's part is $36.4\%$ to $64.5\%$ (Section~\ref{sec:results-localisation-variance-alt}). The split is computed on the ratings alone, so no preprocessing, model, or fusion choice can recover shared signal the ratings do not carry. More visitors would estimate the visitor's part more precisely without turning it into a shared one, and changing the sensor alters little, because the differences between sensors are small beside the differences between visitors.

Two further causes contribute. The sensors record bodily and attentional correlates of affect, not affect, and those correlates also respond to movement, mental load, and scene luminance (Chapter~\ref{chap:related-work}). The link from correlate to reported feeling therefore need not be the same from one visitor to the next, and it is not: where the literature predicts a direction, for instance that the pupil widens with arousal, the observed sign agrees in twelve of twenty-eight cases, a rate indistinguishable from chance (Section~\ref{sec:results-relations-alt}). And the affect is intermittent. Most of a visit is walking, reading, and neutral viewing, yet a rating is required at every second, so the few moments that carry affect are averaged against many that carry little (Chapter~\ref{chap:limitations}).

Studies that elicit affect deliberately, with seated viewers and short, strongly valenced stimuli, report higher figures (Chapter~\ref{chap:related-work}). The rating split is what allows the gap to be attributed to elicitation rather than to the sensors: the stimulus-driven part those designs rely on is close to absent here. The same split can be computed on any collection with ratings and a stimulus label, and its shares will differ wherever the stimuli, the instrument, or the cohort differ. What transfers is the method, not the figures.

One measurement governs how every comparison is read. Two runs of the same model on the same data differ by chance, and that difference, the selection resolution, was fixed at $0.08$ on the continuous score and $0.21$ on the ordinal one before any comparison was made. Almost every difference the thesis reports falls inside it (Sections~\ref{sec:results-families-alt} and~\ref{sec:results-alignment-alt}). The null is therefore robust to configuration, and no configuration is established as the better one.
