\section{Effects of Scoping to the Attended Painting}
\label{sec:discussion-localisation-alt}

blocks.body: Restricting prediction to the seconds in which a visitor attends a painting was the most direct test of stimulus-driven signal, and it found none. With the painting held fixed the painting's part of a rating stays at or below $3.3\%$, training on those seconds lowered the ordinal score on every slice, and none of the 48 paired tests against the whole-session model survives correction (Section~\ref{sec:results-localisation-scoping-alt}). Restricting the rows cannot create shared signal the ratings do not contain. The restriction yielded one thing the scores do not show: the moment of attending a painting is the only point at which two free-roaming visitors' data are comparable, and only there could the visitor's part be shown to dominate with the stimulus held fixed. It also exposed a result that requires care. On retro, which painting is on view accounts for a larger share of every sensor's variation than of the ratings' variation, in part because the retrospective ratings are nearly flat within a visit (Section~\ref{sec:results-localisation-variance-alt}). That is not a recommendation for an affect model. A signal that varies with the painting more than the visitor's rating does is most simply read as measuring the painting, through its luminance and content, a confound this dataset cannot remove.

Recasting the target as a small number of ordered levels did not add signal. The two ways of producing the levels, a classifier trained on them or a continuous prediction binned afterwards, cannot be told apart on this cohort (Section~\ref{sec:results-binning-alt}), and part of any change in an ordinal score comes only from how the levels are distributed, which both the row restriction above and the person-relative target below shift (Chapter~\ref{chap:limitations}). Discretising changes what can be scored without enlarging what is there to score.

Being stable within a person, being shared across people, and carrying affect are three different properties. Heart-rate variability is the signal most locked to the person and produced the single highest score in the thesis, yet averaged over all four slices it does not lead (Section~\ref{sec:results-unimodal-alt}): a stable trait of the individual is informative within a visitor and largely unavailable to a model that has never met that visitor. The same split also says something about the target. Valence and arousal are treated as stimulus-driven quantities on a shared scale, so that two people viewing the same painting should give comparable ratings. Here the painting moves a rating by at most $1.5\%$ and the person sets the rest, so the scale behaves as a person-relative one. Two intermediate levels remain untested: recurring response types across visitors, which a larger cohort could look for, and engagement, which gaze, dwell, and revisit behaviour measure directly and which could be predicted first and related to affect afterwards.

On this evidence a guide cannot rely on second-by-second affect decoding for an unseen visitor, and neither more sensors nor a different way of combining them changes that: the best score any combination reached, $+0.0822$, is exactly the best score a single sensor reached (Section~\ref{sec:results-combination-alt}). How many sensors a visitor wears is a cost decision, not an accuracy one.

Adapting the model to the individual is the remedy a person-specific response most directly motivates. Three levers were tried: subtracting each visitor's resting level from their signals, training on a short labelled warm-up of the visitor's own first ratings, and redefining the rating levels around each visitor's own range. None survived correction, so the outcome is null rather than negative (Section~\ref{sec:results-personalisation-verdict-alt}). The warm-up came closest, and its gain increases with each additional second it is given, but it requires the visitor's own ratings, which a museum cannot request; the resting-level baseline, the one lever a deployment could run without visitor input, moved the pooled figures less consistently. The same fact motivates personalisation and obstructs it. How to obtain the warm-up's apparent gain without its labels is the question Experiment~5 leaves open (Chapter~\ref{chap:conclusion}).

This thesis set out to establish what a multimodal, gaze-aware guide could rely on in a free-roaming \ac{VR} museum, using a preprocessing and feature-engineering pipeline derived from the per-sensor methods literature.

Reliable subject-independent prediction of valence and arousal was not achieved. No sensor, combination of sensors, target representation, scoping of the visit, or personalisation mechanism tested predicted above the chance-corrected floor, so affect is not an input a guide can rely on in a collection of this kind. The affective response in this setting is overwhelmingly individual: between $0.1\%$ and $1.5\%$ of a visitor's rating is shared with other visitors viewing the same painting, against $36.4\%$ to $64.5\%$ carried by a stable trait of that person.

Three findings carry that answer. On this cohort the sensors are not the constraint, since the gap between the leading sensors falls inside the selection resolution. No combination of sensors scores above the best single sensor on either stream. Neither the target representation, nor scoping prediction to the attended painting, nor personalisation moves the result past that resolution, and personalisation's consistent direction across 21 of the 24 cells is an underpowered null, not evidence against adaptation (Section~\ref{sec:results-summary-alt}).

This thesis reaches two conclusions. The first is a measured ceiling. Across every approach evaluated on this collection, five sensors and every combination of them, an ordinal target, scoping prediction to the attended painting, and three personalisation levers, prediction of an unseen visitor's valence or arousal did not rise above the chance-corrected floor, the score a model that knows nothing about the visitor would obtain. Approaches outside that set remain open. The second is the explanation for that ceiling: splitting each rating into a part that belongs to the visitor, a part that belongs to the painting, and a remainder attributes it predominantly to the visitor and only marginally to the painting viewed. Both conclusions also indicate where further work should concentrate. A response this person-specific motivates personalisation, and of the three levers evaluated the labelled warm-up came closest, its gain increasing with each additional second of the visitor's own ratings. The same property limits its use, since those annotations are precisely what a museum cannot request of a visitor.

The ceiling reported here belongs to the data, not to the analysis, which makes the design of the next collection the more consequential choice, ahead of the design of the next model. Three directions answer the limits Chapter~\ref{chap:discussion} identifies: intermittent affect, the cost of labelled personalisation, and the unexplained person component.

\textbf{An event-anchored collection.} The stimulus set is the largest lever, since it is what the shared component is a share of, and five static paintings viewed at leisure yielded a painting share at or below $3.3\%$. A next collection would choose works for the contrast between the responses they provoke, use enough of them that the stimulus effect rests on more than five units, and have every visitor meet every stimulus more than once, so that the person component could be estimated and removed instead of only withheld. The gaze log already resolves sub-painting regions (Section~\ref{sec:results-characterization-alt}), so visitors could be compared around shared events such as a first fixation, a revisit, or a guide utterance, moments at which affect is more plausibly present than at an arbitrary second.

\textbf{Label-efficient personalisation.} The warm-up's ordered response is the clearest direction Experiment~5 produced and the least deployable, since it trains on the visitor's own ratings. The label-free end of the same family is the one to test next: baselines estimated passively from the unlabelled stream, implicit behavioural signals such as dwell, revisits, and conversational engagement in place of ratings, and adaptation that places an unseen visitor relative to the cohort without any labelled second. Where a short labelled warm-up is acceptable, a session in this engine already opens with an eye-tracker calibration step, and extending it briefly would supply the labels without lengthening a setup the visitor already accepts.

\textbf{Cohort, labels, and covariates.} A cohort sized for a paired per-participant test would resolve what personalisation could not settle at this size. The labels deserve the attention that went to the sensors: the two annotation streams do not converge, and the retrospective ratings are close to piecewise-constant, so a single instrument validated against a known elicitation should precede the main collection. Recording demographic, personality, art-familiarity, and affect-disposition covariates would let the $36.4\%$ to $64.5\%$ carried by stable differences between people be modelled instead of left unexplained, and logging scene luminance would let the pupil signal be separated from the light and content of what is viewed.

The variance decomposition that explains this result needs only the ratings and a stimulus label, so a pilot can compute it before any sensor pipeline exists. It answers the question a prediction experiment cannot answer about itself, whether there is a shared response to find at all, and reporting it first would tell a project whether its effort belongs in sensing, in annotation, or in the stimuli.
